payload.name: Resolve deictic time expressions during extraction
payload.description: When a user message states an event happened or an item was received using only a relative time word (yesterday, today, last week, N days ago), during extraction resolve it with the message timestamp and create an event memory.
content: During extraction, if a user message states a concrete event (e.g., receiving/being given something, an occurrence) and gives only a deictic time word such as 'yesterday', 'today', 'this morning', or 'N days ago', compute the absolute date using the message's occurred_at timestamp and create an event candidate (memory kind: event) with that date and the original evidence.

Do not create such a candidate when the statement is just an object mention without an event verb, or when the message already provides an absolute date; in the latter case keep normal extraction with the stated date.
If no occurred_at timestamp is available for the message, do not guess a date; skip the deictic resolution and continue with base extraction.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes drops facts whose only temporal anchor is a relative expression such as 'yesterday', leaving later 'when did X happen' questions unanswerable. This Skill applies when a user message names an event (e.g., receiving a letter) and gives only a deictic time; it resolves that time from the message timestamp and creates an event memory. It must not apply when the text already contains an absolute date or when no usable message timestamp exists, because the base resolution rule already covers those cases.

payload.name: ResolveDeicticReferencesInEventExtraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from a message containing deictic references—relative time phrases ('last Friday', 'yesterday') or first-person plural subjects ('we', 'our')—apply during extraction to resolve absolute dates from occurred_at and preserve all participants.
content: Resolve relative time phrases to absolute dates using the source message's occurred_at timestamp before writing world_start; e.g., 'last Friday' from a Sunday message refers to the Friday two days prior, not the previous day's date.
When the speaker uses 'we' or 'our' for an activity, include all participants (e.g., the speaker and their partner) in the memory content rather than attributing the event only to the speaker.

candidates.solves: Extraction of event memories frequently mishandles deictic references: relative time expressions are assigned incorrect absolute dates, and first-person plural subjects are reduced to the speaker alone, yielding incomplete or wrong memories. This Skill applies during extraction whenever a message like 'we tried ... last Friday' must become an event memory, across any topic. It does not apply when the message states an explicit absolute date or a singular subject, where the base workflow is already sufficient.

payload.name: ExtractEmbeddedPersonalEventsWithResolvedTime
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message mixes a general topic with a specific personal event (trip, visit, activity) and contains a relative time reference like 'last year'; create an event memory for the personal event and resolve the time relative to the message timestamp.
content: When a message contains a specific personal experience (e.g., a trip, visit, or significant activity) embedded in general discussion, extract it as its own event memory instead of only capturing the general topic.

Resolve relative time expressions such as 'last year', 'two months ago', or 'yesterday' against the message's occurred_at timestamp to compute an absolute world_start date; record the resolved date in the event memory.

candidates.solves: Extraction drops specific personal events when the message's main theme is a general reflection, so later questions about the event cannot be answered. Applies when a speaker mentions a discrete past experience (trip, visit, activity) with a relative time word inside casual conversation. Does not apply when the message contains no concrete factual event or when no reliable time reference exists.

payload.name: DistinctEventOccurrencesAddNotUpdate
payload.description: When a candidate event is the same type and subject as an existing event memory but is a separate occurrence (different date, ordinal, venue, or result), before choosing UPDATE, verify whether it is a new instance and ADD a new event memory instead of overwriting the old one.
content: When a candidate event is the same type and subject as an existing event memory but is a separate occurrence (different date, ordinal, venue, or result), ADD a new event memory instead of UPDATING the old one; preserve the prior occurrence's time and details.

Before choosing UPDATE/enrichment, check whether the incoming message describes the same specific occurrence already stored (matching time and place). If it is a new instance, create a new memory; only enrich when the same occurrence gains extra detail.

candidates.solves: The failure is that repeated occurrences of a recurring event type are collapsed into one memory, overwriting earlier instances and making later counts impossible. This Skill applies when a session reports another instance of the same recurring event for the same subject (e.g., a new tournament win) with its own date or ordinal; the agent must store it as a distinct event memory. It does not apply when new text only adds detail to the already-stored occurrence (same time and place), where enrichment is correct.

payload.name: Extract explicit life-event dates from narrative
payload.description: When during construction extraction the speaker explicitly states a year/date for a personal or family life event (wedding, birth, graduation, move) inside emotional or reflective narrative, create an event candidate.
content: During extraction, scan user messages for directly stated dates tied to life events (e.g., 'my parents' wedding in 1993', 'she was born in 1987'). Do not skip these because the surrounding sentence is emotional, nostalgic, or photo-related.

Create one candidate with memory type 'event', subject = the person or persons involved, predicate = the event type (e.g., wedding, birth), and the stated date as the event date. Anchor to session timestamp only if no explicit date is given.

Stop after extracting the explicitly stated fact; do not infer dates from vague references, do not extract the same fact from later rephrasings, and do not treat a date attached only to a photo or object as a life-event date.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes skips explicitly stated dates for personal or family life events (weddings, births, graduations, moves) when they appear inside emotional, nostalgic, or reflective narrative, causing the fact to be missing from memory. This skill applies in future sessions where a speaker directly asserts a year or date for such a life event, even if the surrounding text is not factual-sounding. It must not apply when no explicit date is asserted, or when the date refers only to a photo, object, or non-life-event context.

payload.name: RecordPastCompletedEventsFromRelativeTime
payload.description: Use when a user/entity statement describes an activity completed at an explicit past relative time (e.g., 'two weeks ago I read...', 'last month I finished...'). Apply during extraction to record the completed event with a resolved date, not as a current ongoing state.
content: When a message contains an explicit past-time reference (e.g., '<N> ago', 'last ...', 'in <past month/year>') tied to a completed activity verb (read, watched, visited, finished, etc.), extract a memory of kind `event` (or a completed `state`) whose world_start/world_end reflects the resolved past date, computed from the message timestamp; do not label it 'currently' or as ongoing.
Keep a past completed activity in its own memory; do not merge it with memories describing current ongoing activities. If the message also states a current activity, extract that separately.
Stop when the verb indicates a present ongoing action (e.g., 'I am reading', 'currently') or when no explicit past time anchor is present, since the base policy already handles current states.

candidates.solves: The failure mechanism is extracting a past completed activity, anchored by a relative time phrase, as an ongoing state, which loses the completion date. This Skill applies when a future session contains an utterance like 'two weeks ago I read X' or 'last month I finished Y', and the construction agent must record the completed event with its resolved past date so later questions about that period can be answered. It does not apply to present-tense ongoing activities ('I am currently reading X'), which the base policy already stores as current states.

payload.name: Recurring event interval extraction
payload.description: When a message describes a repeated event for the same person (e.g., another doctor appointment, trip, or birthday) and an earlier occurrence already exists in memory, extract the time elapsed between the two occurrences when it is computable from timestamps.
content: During extraction, if the message mentions a second or later occurrence of an event type already stored for the same subject (e.g., appointment, trip, class), compare it against prior occurrences and compute the interval from session timestamps or explicit dates.

If the interval is derivable and the repeated occurrence is contextually significant, add a relationship memory capturing the gap (e.g., 'first and second appointments were N months apart') in addition to the new event memory; otherwise keep the event memory alone.
Do not generate intervals for one-off events, unrelated event pairs, or when the gap cannot be resolved; stop after comparing with the most recent prior occurrence.

candidates.solves: The construction agent stores repeated events in isolation and omits the temporal relationship between them, so later questions about elapsed time between occurrences cannot be answered. Applies when a message introduces a second or later instance of an event type already in memory for the same subject and the interval is computable. Not for one-off events, unrelated pairs, or when no earlier occurrence exists.

payload.name: Resolve-relative-time-dates-in-event-extraction
payload.description: When extracting event memories from messages containing relative time phrases like 'last week', 'yesterday', or 'a month ago', resolve the event world_start relative to the message/session timestamp instead of using the message's own date.
content: During extraction, when a message describes an event with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'last month', 'a week ago'), resolve the reference date by subtracting the period from the message/session timestamp and use that resolved date as world_start; never use the message date itself.
Prefer a concrete resolved date in the memory content; you may keep a short relative qualifier only if it clarifies recency, but the stored date must be the offset date.

If a later message supplies an explicit date for the same event, update the existing memory to that explicit date (do not add a duplicate); do not apply this rule to absolute dates or to non-temporal uses of 'last' (e.g., 'my last tournament').

candidates.solves: When constructing event memories from messages with deictic time expressions (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'a week ago'), models often set world_start to the message timestamp date instead of the offset date, corrupting the fact. This Skill applies during extraction of event memories whenever a source message contains a relative time phrase and requires computing the resolved date from the message/session timestamp. It must not be used for absolute dates, for sequence-relative phrases like 'my last tournament', or for updates that restate an existing event without a new date.

payload.name: Update ongoing event on completion
payload.description: When a later message describes the completion or end of an activity that was previously stored as an ongoing event without an end time, during extraction and CRUD use the existing memory and update its world_end or duration instead of ADDing a separate completion event.
content: During extraction, when a candidate describes the completion of an activity, search the existing memory pool for an event memory of the same subject and activity with world_end null.

If a matching ongoing event exists, represent the completion as an UPDATE of that memory: set world_end from the message timestamp or stated completion time, and include the duration if inferable; do not ADD a separate completion event.
Only ADD a new event if no matching ongoing event exists or the activity is clearly different.

candidates.solves: Fixes missing durations/end times when a speaker later reports finishing an activity that was stored earlier as an ongoing event. Applies when a future session message states completion of a previously recorded ongoing event with the same subject and activity; the agent should UPDATE the existing event memory with the end date or duration rather than ADD a new completion event. Does not apply when the later message describes a genuinely new or different activity, or when no prior ongoing-event memory exists.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeWeekendDateRanges
payload.description: When extracting an event whose time is stated as 'last weekend', 'this weekend', or 'next weekend' relative to the message timestamp, use this to resolve the correct Saturday-Sunday range before storing the memory.
content: When a candidate event contains a relative weekend phrase ('last weekend', 'this weekend', 'next weekend'), resolve it against the message timestamp as a Saturday-to-Sunday range: 'last weekend' = the Sat-Sun immediately preceding the message date; 'this weekend' = the Sat-Sun containing the message date if it falls on Sat/Sun, otherwise the upcoming Sat-Sun; 'next weekend' = the Sat-Sun after 'this weekend'. Never include Monday in the weekend range.

Store the resolved Saturday and Sunday dates in world_start/world_end and in the memory content. If the intended weekend is ambiguous, preserve the source phrase in the content instead of inventing a shifted date.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes miscalculates relative weekend references, shifting events by a day (e.g., treating 'last weekend' as Sunday-Monday instead of Saturday-Sunday). This Skill applies when constructing event memories from messages that use 'last/this/next weekend' and need a Saturday-Sunday range anchored to the message timestamp. It does not apply to absolute dates, named holidays, or multi-day events that are not weekend-relative.

payload.name: Resolve relative dates to absolute event dates
payload.description: Use when extracting event memories and the source message states a relative time (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday', 'three days ago') with a known message/session timestamp; resolve it to the actual date for world_start instead of using the message timestamp.
content: During extraction, when an event's timing comes from a relative expression (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday', 'a couple of days ago') and the message/session timestamp provides the anchor, resolve the expression to its actual calendar date (using the message timestamp, not the current date) and set world_start to that resolved date; do not use the message timestamp as the event date.
Keep the relative wording in the memory content only as a secondary cue; the resolved absolute date belongs in world_start so the event remains retrievable by date.
When later updating an existing memory, do not overwrite world_start with the new message's timestamp unless that new message itself explicitly re-dates the same event.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that relative time phrases are treated as calendar facts or collapsed to the message timestamp, so event memories lose their true date anchoring. The concrete future pattern is construction of an event memory from a message that uses 'last Friday', 'yesterday', or similar relative terms with a known message timestamp. It must not apply when the message gives an explicit date or when the relative expression cannot be resolved to a specific day.

payload.name: Resolve relative dates in memory content
payload.description: When extracting or updating memories, if a plan/event claim uses a relative calendar phrase such as 'next month' or 'tomorrow' that can be anchored to the message/session timestamp, replace it with the absolute date in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a candidate memory's content contains a relative calendar expression (e.g., 'next month', 'tomorrow', 'last week', 'this Friday') and the source message has a timestamp, resolve the expression to an absolute date (e.g., 'September 2023', '2023-09-01') in the content string, and align world_start/world_end with that date.

Do not keep the relative phrase in the final memory content when the absolute anchor is known; the memory must be answerable on its own. If no reliable anchor exists or the expression is vague (e.g., 'someday'), retain the phrase and do not invent a date.

candidates.solves: A construction agent often extracts a plan or event claim, computes world_start from a relative phrase like 'next month', but leaves the relative phrase in the content, so later questions about the date cannot be answered from memory. This Skill applies when a candidate memory for a future plan/event contains a calendar-relative expression anchored to the message timestamp; it resolves that expression to an absolute date in the content. It does not apply when the expression has no clear temporal anchor or the timestamp is unavailable.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeDurationToAbsoluteYear
payload.description: When a message includes a numeric relative duration (e.g., 'for 3 years') and a message/session timestamp is available, compute and store the implied absolute start year during memory extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message states a concrete duration (e.g., 'for N years/months') and the message/session timestamp is known, compute the implied start date/year by subtracting the duration from the timestamp.
Store both the original duration and the resolved absolute date in the candidate content, e.g., 'has had them for 3 years (since 2020)'. Use the resolved year when the duration is in years.
Do not convert vague time references without a number (e.g., 'a while', 'several years'); record only what is explicitly stated.

candidates.solves: When a user reports a numeric relative duration (e.g., 'for 3 years') in a dated message, memory extraction often stores only the duration and omits the implied absolute start year, so future 'when did X start/begin' questions cannot be answered. This Skill applies during extraction to derive the start year from the message/session timestamp and include it in the memory content while preserving the original duration. It must not be used for vague durations without a number or for messages that already contain an explicit start date.

payload.name: Extract past-event memories from assistant turns
payload.description: Use during candidate extraction when an assistant message states a first-person past event (e.g., a trip, visit, or vacation) with an explicit time reference and a place; create an event memory candidate with the time resolved from the message timestamp.
content: When an assistant message describes a first-person past event with an explicit time reference (e.g., 'last summer', 'in 2022'), create an event memory candidate; do not skip it because the speaker is the user.
Resolve relative time expressions ('last summer', 'last year') against the message timestamp to an absolute time (e.g., summer 2022) before storing.
Record the event compactly with the mentioned location and resolved time; do not add unstated details or run extra searches.

candidates.solves: The failure mechanism is that explicit autobiographical event claims in assistant messages, such as a vacation to a place at a resolved past time, are skipped during extraction, so no memory candidate is produced and the fact is lost. This Skill applies when an assistant turn states a first-person past event with a temporal expression and a place. It does not apply to third-party events, hypotheticals, or statements without an explicit time reference.

payload.name: Resolve relative event dates from message timestamp
payload.description: When extracting an event memory and the message contains a relative time expression such as 'yesterday' or 'last week', resolve the actual event date from the message occurred_at timestamp and use it for world_start.
content: When a message describes an event with a relative time reference (e.g., 'yesterday', 'last week', 'two days ago'), compute the absolute event date using the message's occurred_at timestamp and set world_start to that computed date, not the message timestamp.
Record the resolved date in the memory content when it clarifies the event (e.g., 'met Anna on 31 January 2023') so the date is not lost.
Do not apply this rule when the event occurs at the message time (e.g., 'today', 'now') or when no relative time expression is present.

candidates.solves: Construction agents often store the message timestamp as the event date when a user describes a past event with a relative time expression like 'yesterday' or 'last week', losing the true date. This Skill applies to any future session where an event memory is extracted and the message contains a relative time reference that can be resolved against the message's occurred_at timestamp; it computes the absolute event date for world_start. It does not apply when the event occurs at the message time (e.g., 'today') or when no relative expression is present.

payload.name: PreserveDistinctEventDatesOnUpdate
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing event memory with a new event whose resolved date differs from the memory's current world_start, during extraction or CRUD, create a separate event memory or keep the new event's resolved date instead of overwriting the existing date.
content: Resolve relative dates (e.g., 'last weekend') from the message/session timestamp and keep the resolved date in the candidate's world_start.

During UPDATE of an event memory, if the new event's resolved date differs from the existing memory's world_start, do not replace world_start with a conflicting date; create a new separate event memory for the new event with its own resolved date.
Only enrich an existing event memory when the new details refer to the same event and date already captured; otherwise the events have different dates and must not share one world_start.

candidates.solves: Construction UPDATE can corrupt an event memory's date by overwriting world_start with an unrelated value when a new message describes a distinct event with a relative time (e.g., 'last weekend'), causing recall errors. Applies when a candidate event's resolved date differs from the existing memory's world_start; create a separate memory for the new dated event instead of merging dates. Does not apply when new details concern the same event/date already in memory, where normal UPDATE is sufficient.

payload.name: Resolve relative time expressions in event extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event from a timestamped source message that describes it with a relative time phrase such as 'last week' or 'yesterday', use this Skill to convert the phrase to explicit calendar dates and record them in the candidate.
content: During extraction, when a source message uses a relative time expression (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'this month') and has an occurred_at timestamp, resolve the expression to explicit calendar dates before writing the candidate.

Store the resolved dates in the event content (e.g., mention the month/year) and set world_start and world_end to the first and last day of that resolved period; do not preserve the bare relative phrase as the only time reference.
Stop after resolving that expression; do not add further temporal inference or expand the candidate beyond the stated event.

candidates.solves: Events from messages with relative time phrases like 'last week' often keep the phrase and set world_start from the processing date, losing the month/year. Apply when a timestamped source message describes an event using a relative time expression: resolve it to explicit dates, include them in content, and set world_start/world_end from that range. Do not apply when the message already has absolute dates or the expression is unresolvable.

payload.name: ExtractSecondaryRelativeTimeEvents
payload.description: When a message during construction extraction contains a clause stating the speaker participated in an event with others on a relative past day (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday'), create a separate event memory with the resolved absolute date even if the main topic is different.
content: During extraction, scan clauses for relative past-time event statements (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday') naming an activity and subject. If found and the activity is a concrete personal event, create a separate 'event' memory with subject, resolved date computed from the message timestamp, and participants if mentioned. Do not merge it into unrelated existing memories. Stop after capturing clearly stated events; do not infer events from opinions or general statements.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can omit a speaker's personal event when it appears as a secondary clause with a relative time (e.g., 'last Friday') in a message otherwise about encouragement or another topic. Future sessions may ask about that event date. This Skill applies when a message states a concrete past activity with a relative weekday/time anchor and identifiable subject; it does not apply to opinions, hypotheticals, or statements without a specific event-time anchor.

payload.name: ResolveRelativeTimeInMemoryContent
payload.description: Use when extracting or updating event/state memories from messages with relative calendar expressions such as yesterday, last week, last month, or N days ago; replace them in memory content with the absolute date derived from the message timestamp.
content: When a source message uses a relative calendar expression (yesterday, last week, last month, last year, N days/weeks/months ago), resolve it against the message/session timestamp to a concrete date (e.g., 'May 2023') and use that absolute date in the memory content; do not leave the relative phrase in the content.
Apply this both when forming an extraction candidate and when updating or merging an existing event or state memory in CRUD.
Set world_start to the computed date for events and states; keep world_end null unless the source specifies a duration or end date.

If the expression cannot be precisely anchored (e.g., 'recently', 'a while ago'), retain the vague wording but still set world_start from the timestamp and avoid stating a more specific date than the source supports.

candidates.solves: General failure: relative time expressions such as 'last month' are written verbatim into memory content while only world_start is resolved, so later recall loses the concrete date. This skill applies when constructing or updating event/state memories from messages that contain calendar-relative expressions and a known message timestamp; it must not apply to vague, unanchored expressions like 'recently' or to non-temporal memory kinds such as profiles and relationships.

payload.name: ExtractSpeakerPastActions
payload.description: When a message contains a speaker's own first-person past action (e.g., 'I made ... last week') alongside another subject or topic, generate a separate event candidate for it and resolve relative time from the message timestamp. Applies during extraction.
content: During extraction, identify each distinct first-person past action by the current speaker (e.g., 'I made ...', 'I went ...', 'I cooked ...') even if the surrounding message mainly discusses another person's experience or a broader topic.

Create a separate event candidate for each such action with subject set to the speaker; state the action and the relative time expression as given, then resolve relative time using the message's occurred_at timestamp (e.g., 'last week' becomes that calendar week).
Do not suppress a speaker's own event because the same message already produced candidates for other subjects; one message can yield multiple independent events.

Stop after one event candidate per distinct speaker action; do not extract when the action is already captured in the same message or when the statement is only an opinion, plan, preference, or vague routine.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often drops a speaker's own past action (e.g., 'I made ... last week') when the same message centers on another person's story or an unrelated topic, so that action never becomes a durable event. Applies to future messages containing a first-person past-action statement alongside other subjects; the Skill forces a separate event candidate with time resolved from the message timestamp. Not for already-captured actions or non-specific opinions, plans, or routine statements.

payload.name: ExtractEventFromRelativeTimeMention
payload.description: When a user mentions attending an event, meetup, or activity with a relative time phrase (e.g., last week, recently), extract an event memory during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a user states they attended an event, meetup, gathering, or activity with a relative time reference (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'recently'), create a candidate event memory.
Resolve the relative time from the message/session timestamp to a concrete date or date range.

If the user describes the event's purpose or theme (e.g., 'to support each other'), include it briefly in the description; do not invent a specific event name beyond what is stated. Do not apply to future plans, hypothetical events, or explicit non-attendance.

candidates.solves: Extraction fails when a user mentions an attended event using relative time and informal wording, producing no memory. This Skill applies to any message where the user references having gone to an event, meetup, or activity in a relative past timeframe, and instructs extracting an event memory with resolved date. It must not apply to future plans, hypothetical events, or messages with no event reference.

payload.name: Resolve Weekday Event Dates in Memories
payload.description: When extracting or adding an event memory, if a message reports an event with a relative time phrase like 'On Friday' or 'yesterday' and the message has a timestamp, resolve that phrase to a concrete calendar date and include the date in the memory content.
content: During extraction, when a speaker reports a past event using a weekday or other relative time phrase (e.g., 'On Friday', 'last week', 'yesterday'), compute the exact calendar date from the message timestamp and include that date in the memory content, not just in future-planning fields.
During CRUD, when adding or updating such an event memory, preserve the resolved date in the memory content and set world_start to it if the date is the event's occurrence time.

Stop after resolving the one date the phrase refers to; do not invent or expand to additional dates unless the source explicitly provides them, and do not apply this to relative phrases that only describe future plans rather than the event's occurrence.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes drops an event's concrete date when it is stated only as a weekday/relative phrase (e.g., 'On Friday'), making later date questions unanswerable. This Skill applies when a timestamped message reports an event with such a phrase; resolve it to the exact calendar date and store it in the event memory. It does not apply when the message already has an explicit date or when the phrase only describes a future plan.

payload.name: Resolve relative timing in event extraction
payload.description: When extracting event memories from messages that state when something happened using a relative expression (last week, yesterday, a few days ago), resolve it against the message timestamp and record the resolved date in the memory content.
content: When a message uses a relative time phrase to describe when a past event happened (e.g., 'last week', 'yesterday', 'two days ago'), resolve it to a calendar date using the message's timestamp and include both the phrase and the resolved date in the event memory content.
Set the event memory's world_start to the resolved event-occurrence date (not the message date) when the phrase points earlier, and keep the original phrase for traceability.
Apply only to one-off events explicitly timed relative to the message; skip phrases that describe recurring habits or states with no distinct calendar anchoring.

candidates.solves: Future questions asking when a past event happened are unanswerable when extraction keeps the event but drops relative timing phrases ('last week', 'yesterday'). Apply when a message describes a single past event using such a phrase: resolve it against the message timestamp and store both the phrase and the resolved date. Do not apply when no temporal qualifier is present, when the event occurs at message time, or when the phrase describes a repeating habit.

payload.name: Store intervals between related events
payload.description: When a message introduces a new event for a subject who already has a stored event of the same type and both event dates are known, during extraction also record the elapsed time between them.
content: During extraction, when a message introduces a new event for a subject who already has a stored event of the same type (e.g., a second adoption or relocation) and both event dates are known, also extract a candidate memory of kind 'event' recording the elapsed time between the two events, e.g., 'three months passed between the first and second adoption'.

Only create this interval memory when the two events are directly comparable (same subject, same event type) and their dates are present in the message or existing memory; skip it when events are unrelated, either date is unknown, or the interval is already stored.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a message introduces a new event that matches a previously stored event of the same type for the same subject and both event dates are known, also add a concise event memory for the elapsed time between them. Applies to future sessions where a later message reveals a second comparable event and a question may ask how much time passed between them. Does not apply when events are unrelated, dates are missing, or the interval is already recorded.

payload.name: Resolve relative-time references to prior plans during extraction
payload.description: When a message uses a relative time (tomorrow, next week) to confirm or schedule a plan/event mentioned earlier in the session, resolve the date from the message timestamp and extract or update the plan memory.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a relative time reference (e.g., 'tomorrow', 'next week') that confirms or sets the date of a plan/event already discussed earlier in the session, resolve the reference against the message timestamp to an absolute date and generate an extraction candidate for that plan/event.
Use the earlier plan description from the session as the memory content/evidence, and attach the current message as an additional source; do not create a new memory for the relative phrase alone.
Skip extraction if the referenced plan is already stored with the same resolved date, or if the relative time does not refer to any previously discussed plan/event.

candidates.solves: This solves missed extraction of plan dates when users confirm plans with relative time without restating the plan. Future pattern: a session contains an earlier plan mention and later a message like 'see you tomorrow'; the agent must produce a dated plan/event candidate. It must not apply to casual relative time not tied to a prior plan or to plans already stored with the same date.

payload.name: Extract events with relative time references
payload.description: When a message states a past event using a relative time expression (e.g., 'last Friday', 'yesterday', 'two weeks ago'), use it during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, when a user message describes an action or event that happened at a relative time (last Friday, yesterday, this morning, N days/weeks ago), generate an `event` candidate.
Resolve the relative time against the message timestamp (or session timestamp if message timestamp is absent) to a concrete date.
Attribute the event to the speaker of the message, and include the activity and the resolved date in the candidate.
Do not create such candidates for hypothetical, future, or non-factual statements, or when the relative time cannot be resolved.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes drops clear statements of past events when the time is given relatively, leaving memory empty for later temporal questions. Applies to future sessions where a speaker reports an event with a relative date such as 'last Friday' or 'yesterday' and a later question asks when it happened. Does not apply to preferences, hypothetical statements, or messages without a resolvable relative time, where base extraction rules already suffice.

payload.name: Verify Memory Exists Before SKIP
payload.description: When deciding whether to SKIP a constructed memory candidate during CRUD, if the candidate's core assertion has no matching version in the retrieved existing memory pool, choose ADD instead of SKIP.
content: Before choosing SKIP for a candidate, confirm that at least one retrieved existing memory actually contains the candidate's core assertion (same subject, predicate, and object, or a semantically equivalent phrasing).
If no existing memory matches the core assertion, do not SKIP; select ADD (or MERGE only when the existing memory is missing details) so the evidence-backed fact is persisted.
If an existing memory already expresses the same fact, SKIP or MERGE is still allowed; never add a duplicate or unnecessarily expand an existing memory.

candidates.solves: Construction Agents sometimes SKIP a candidate on the assumption that it is already represented in memory even though no retrieved existing memory actually contains the asserted fact, so the fact is never persisted. Apply when a candidate's core assertion (subject, predicate, and object) has no matching version in the retrieved existing-memory pool: ADD it instead of SKIP. Do not apply when an existing memory version already expresses the same fact; in that case SKIP or MERGE remains correct.

payload.name: Verify existing memory before SKIP as duplicate
payload.description: Use during construction decision stage when an extraction candidate is about to be skipped because it seems duplicate or already represented; apply before finalizing the decision.
content: Before choosing SKIP with reason 'duplicate or already fully represented', verify that the retrieved existing-memory pool actually contains a memory whose subject and content cover the candidate's full claim. If no covering memory is present — including when the pool is empty — do not SKIP; record the candidate as a new memory with ADD (or use UPDATE/MERGE only when a partial covering memory exists).
A candidate cannot be 'already represented' by an absent memory; missing coverage is an add signal, not a skip signal.

candidates.solves: Fixes false-duplicate SKIPs during construction decisions: a candidate is skipped with reason 'duplicate or already fully represented' even though the existing-memory pool contains no covering memory, so the fact is never stored. Applies whenever a construction candidate is evaluated for SKIP based on duplication; require positive evidence of a covering memory before skipping. Not applicable when a genuinely covering memory exists or when the candidate is not a valid memory candidate.

payload.name: Verify memory coverage before skipping candidates
payload.description: Apply during Construction CRUD when a candidate is skipped with the reason that its information is already included in an updated memory, or when several distinct facts from one message are skipped as duplicates.
content: During CRUD decisions, before SKIP for reason 'already included in an updated memory', verify the covering memory is an existing committed memory from the retrieval pool or a memory returned by an earlier ADD/UPDATE in the current batch. A mere candidate from the same extraction batch is not sufficient coverage.

When a single user message states several distinct facts (e.g., multiple motivations, attributes, or preferences), add a separate memory for each distinct fact. Do not skip a candidate just because another candidate seems similar unless the other memory is actually committed or created in this batch and fully subsumes it.

candidates.solves: This solves the failure where Construction CRUD skips extracted facts as 'already included in an updated memory' even though no committed or newly created memory covers them, so distinct facts are silently lost. It applies to future sessions where a message expresses multiple distinct facts and candidates are skipped based on another candidate or a nonexistent updated memory. It must not apply when a candidate genuinely duplicates an existing committed memory or a memory created earlier in the same batch.

payload.name: DistinctFactNotOverlapSkip
payload.description: Apply during construction CRUD decisions when a candidate memory describes a new distinct entity, event, or work that shares only a broad topic, category, or actor with an existing memory, before choosing SKIP or MERGE for apparent overlap.
content: Before SKIPping or MERGEing a candidate as overlapping, verify that the existing memory covers the same specific fact, entity, or claim; sharing only the same broad subject, category, or person is not overlap.

If the candidate introduces a distinct concrete object (such as a different written work, project, event, or item) with its own details, ADD it as a separate memory instead of discarding it; when only part matches, merge only the matching portion and preserve the new distinct fact.

candidates.solves: Fixes construction decisions that wrongly SKIP or MERGE a new durable fact because the candidate shares only a broad topic, category, or actor with an existing memory. Applies when a future candidate describes a distinct concrete entity, event, or work (e.g., a different project, item, or written work) that merely belongs to the same general subject or person as an existing memory; it must not apply to true restatements of the same fact, which should still be merged or skipped.

payload.name: Decision-Stage Redundancy Verification
payload.description: When deciding ADD, UPDATE, MERGE, or SKIP for a candidate memory, use this if the decision reason claims the candidate is already covered by an existing memory; verify the covering memory is present in the current related-memory pool before skipping or merging.
content: Before applying SKIP or MERGE to a candidate because it is already covered, locate the covering memory in the current retrieved related-memory pool.
If no retrieved memory contains the same subject and fact, treat the candidate as new information and ADD it.
Do not infer coverage from group or organizational membership or from topically related but non-identical facts; the existing memory must explicitly state the fact being added.

candidates.solves: The Construction decision stage skipped a valid candidate by citing an existing memory that was not actually present in the retrieved related-memory pool, causing evidence-bound facts to be lost. This Skill applies when a SKIP/UPDATE/MERGE decision is justified by claimed redundancy with a memory that is absent from the current pool; the agent must verify the covering memory exists and otherwise ADD the candidate. It does not apply when the covering memory is genuinely present and normal redundancy rules should be followed.

payload.name: Verify-duplicate-before-skip
payload.description: When deciding between ADD and SKIP for a candidate in the Construction Agent, use when the candidate is marked duplicate or update_type is add and you are considering skipping because existing memory allegedly covers it.
content: Before SKIPping a candidate as a duplicate, verify that the retrieved existing-memory pool actually contains a memory that fully represents the same fact with matching subject and predicate; if no such memory is present or the pool is empty, perform ADD instead.

Do not skip an add candidate merely because it seems familiar, seems implied by another claim, or because the same speaker mentioned similar content earlier; the pool is the only source of truth for duplicates.

candidates.solves: The general failure is skipping new candidate events as duplicates when the memory pool contains no corresponding memory, causing facts to be omitted. Applies to any construction session where a candidate with update_type add is skipped with a duplicate reason while the retrieved pool lacks the equivalent memory; in that case, the agent must ADD. Not applicable when a matching memory genuinely exists in the pool and SKIP/MERGE is appropriate.

payload.name: Preserve New Claims on Partial Memory Overlap
payload.description: When, during construction CRUD decisions, a candidate memory only partially overlaps an existing memory but adds a new claim (e.g., emotional state, evaluation, relationship detail), use UPDATE/MERGE or ADD instead of SKIP.
content: During CRUD decisions, before choosing SKIP, compare every assertion in the candidate against the existing memory; SKIP only when all candidate claims are already present or fully implied.

When a candidate shares some facts with an existing memory but adds any new claim (such as an emotional state, evaluation, or relationship detail), preserve the new claim by UPDATING/MERGING the existing memory or ADDING a separate compact memory; never discard the new claim because one overlapping aspect is represented.
Stop after adding the new claim; do not expand related memories or create redundant entries for facts already present.

candidates.solves: When a Construction candidate partially overlaps an existing memory on one aspect (e.g., ownership) but also asserts a new distinct claim (e.g., a feeling or quality), the decision stage may wrongly SKIP because the old memory seems to cover it, losing the new fact. This Skill applies when a future extracted candidate matches an existing memory on some facts yet adds a new claim that should be preserved via UPDATE/MERGE or ADD. It does not apply when the candidate is fully redundant and SKIP is correct, and it never requires expanding memories beyond the evidence.

payload.name: Confirm Duplicate Before Skipping Candidate
payload.description: Apply during CRUD when a candidate memory is about to be SKIPPED with a reason such as 'already represented' or 'duplicate'; verify that the retrieved existing-memory pool actually contains that information before deciding to skip.
content: During the CRUD/decision stage, before issuing SKIP because a candidate is 'already represented' or a 'duplicate', check the retrieved existing-memory pool. If no existing memory contains the same fact or its paraphrase, do not skip; issue ADD for the candidate. Only SKIP or MERGE when an equivalent memory is actually present in the retrieved pool.

candidates.solves: A candidate memory is sometimes skipped as 'already represented' even when no existing memory contains that fact, causing the information to be lost. This applies when a future session extracts a new memory and the CRUD decision would SKIP it on duplication grounds. It does not apply when the retrieved existing-memory pool genuinely contains an equivalent memory.

payload.name: Verify existing memory before skipping candidate as duplicate
payload.description: When deciding whether to SKIP or MERGE a candidate during construction, apply this before finalizing the action; trigger whenever the candidate is marked 'duplicate' or 'already represented' and the retrieved memory pool or snapshot memories contain no substantively matching memory.
content: Before choosing SKIP with a 'duplicate' reason, verify that the retrieved existing-memory pool and snapshot memories contain at least one memory version whose subject, predicate, and time window substantively cover the candidate. If no such memory exists, the candidate is new.

When the candidate is not substantively covered by any existing memory version ID, ADD it as a new memory; do not infer duplication from similar wording in the source message or from an earlier turn that produced no persisted memory.
Only allow SKIP/MERGE when you can point to the specific existing memory ID(s) that already represent the candidate's content.

candidates.solves: During construction decision-making, the model sometimes marks a candidate as 'duplicate' and SKIPs it even though the retrieved existing-memory pool and snapshot are empty, causing new facts to be lost. This Skill applies when a candidate is a new event/state/relationship and no existing memory version substantively covers its subject+predicate+time; in that case the candidate must be ADDed. It must not apply when the pool actually contains a matching memory, in which case MERGE/UPDATE/SKIP remains correct.

payload.name: Check specific facts before SKIP/MERGE duplicate
payload.description: Use when deciding whether to SKIP or MERGE a construction candidate that seems to duplicate existing memories; verify that every specific factual claim is already present, since sharing only a topic or context is not duplication.
content: When a candidate seems duplicated, list its specific factual claims (subject, action, named item/pose, place, time) and confirm each is present in the retrieved memory pool or already accepted in this batch before skipping.
If the candidate overlaps an existing memory only in topic or context but adds any new specific detail, ADD it or MERGE it into the closest memory; never SKIP it as duplicate.
Stop verification once all specific claims are found; SKIP or MERGE only when the candidate repeats exactly the same specific facts already stored.

candidates.solves: A CRUD decision SKIPs a valid candidate as duplicate when no existing memory contains its specific claims; thematic overlap is mistaken for coverage. Applies when a candidate shares a subject/activity with prior memories but adds a distinct specific detail (new pose, item, place, occurrence). Does not apply when the candidate fully repeats the same specific facts already stored; SKIP/MERGE remains correct.

payload.name: Extract encouragement after setbacks
payload.description: When a speaker offers encouragement, reassurance, or advice to persist after a listener's setback or failure, during extraction and CRUD.
content: When a speaker responds to a listener's setback with explicit encouragement, reassurance, or advice to persist, capture the core gist as a candidate memory that records the speaker, listener, and the substance of the encouragement (e.g., rejections don't define you, keep trying, you'll find the right opportunity).
During CRUD, if no memory of that encouragement exists, create it as a relationship or event memory; if a partial version exists, update it with the missing outlook or advice.
Stop after the core encouragement; do not extract generic pleasantries, greetings, or unsupported factual claims.

candidates.solves: Extraction skips expressive support statements (encouragement, reassurance, advice after a setback) because they are not objective facts, losing what one person told another. Apply when a speaker explicitly responds to a listener's setback with reassurance, persistence advice, or positive outlook; extract the gist as a relationship/event memory and create it if absent. Do not apply to factual claims, greetings, or filler.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Motivation Statements
payload.description: When a message explicitly states the reason or motivation behind a behavior, commitment, or ongoing activity (e.g., 'what keeps me going', 'motivates me', 'I keep doing X because'), use that stated reason as the core of the extracted or updated memory content rather than only the surrounding feelings.
content: During extraction, when a message contains an explicit motivational or causal statement such as '...is what keeps me going', '...motivates me', or 'I keep doing X because...', capture the stated reason as an explicit clause or separate claim in the candidate; do not replace it with only emotional or evaluative paraphrases.
During CRUD updates, when enriching or merging an existing memory, carry forward any explicitly stated motivation from the source message; prune only redundant detail, not the stated reason itself.
Apply only to motivations explicitly stated by the speaker; do not infer hidden motives, and stop once the stated reason is captured.

candidates.solves: Users often state why they persist or value something explicitly; extraction may paraphrase the emotional context and drop the stated reason, so the memory never holds the fact needed to answer later 'what motivates X' questions. This Skill applies to future messages where a speaker explicitly states what motivates or keeps them going while creating or updating a memory. It must not apply when no stated reason exists and motivation would require inference.

payload.name: Extract idiomatic commitment statements
payload.description: When a speaker states their own intention or commitment using idiomatic or negated phrasing such as 'not giving up', 'won't stop', or 'keep going', extract a memory capturing the underlying action.
content: During extraction, treat statements where a person says they will or won't do something, including idiomatic or negated equivalents, as candidates for a 'state' or 'plan' memory (e.g., [person] intends to / not to [action]).

Resolve the idiomatic expression to its concrete action (e.g., 'not giving up' -> not quit) and link the memory to the source message. Only apply when the statement is a personal commitment about a future course of action.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes misses a person's stated commitment when it is phrased idiomatically or with negation (e.g., 'I'm not giving up'), so the fact is never stored. This skill applies when a speaker tells someone their own intended course of action using such indirect phrasing; extract it as a state/plan memory. It should not apply to direct explicit statements the base extractor already handles, nor to purely affective remarks with no concrete action.

payload.name: Preserve image-sharing action from provenance references
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message where the speaker credits or describes a picture/image they shared (e.g., 'That picture is from...', 'This was made by...'), use this Skill to record the sharing event and its source.
content: If a user message refers to a previously shared picture or image and states its creator/provenance (e.g., 'That picture is from X'), extract an event memory that the user shared that picture, including the creator/source as a detail.

Do not convert the picture's source into ownership of a physical themed object (e.g., a bookshelf or decoration) unless the message explicitly states the user owns such an object; do not infer physical objects from figurative praise.

During CRUD, if an existing memory records an inferred ownership but the evidence only supports a sharing event, ADD the sharing event or UPDATE the memory to include the sharing action so the shared picture's provenance is not lost.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often drops the sharing action when a user credits a picture they shared (e.g., 'That picture is from X'), instead hallucinating an ownership event about a themed physical object. This Skill applies when a message references a shared image and states its provenance, and instructs extracting the picture-sharing event with its source while avoiding inferred physical-object ownership. It does not apply when the user explicitly states they own an item, where an ownership/possession memory remains correct.

payload.name: Extract implicit photo-sharing from 'Here are' cues
payload.description: When a message uses 'Here are/is' to present physical items the speaker made or has, without naming a photo, extract that the speaker shared a photo of those items.
content: During extraction, if a speaker presents physical items with 'Here are/is' (e.g., 'Here are some bowls I made') and no photo/picture word appears, include a memory/event that the speaker shared a photo of those items, alongside facts about making/possession.
Do not apply this when 'Here are/is' introduces abstract content (steps, thoughts, lists) or when the message already explicitly mentions sharing a photo; rely on the base policy in those cases.

candidates.solves: Candidates extracted from messages where a speaker says 'Here are ...' for tangible items they created often keep the creation fact but drop the displayed photo-sharing fact, making future 'shared a photo of' questions unanswerable. This Skill applies when future questions ask what someone shared a photo of and the evidence contains a deictic presentation of physical objects. It must not apply to 'Here are' phrases about abstract lists or already explicit photo mentions.

payload.name: Extract explicit first-person feelings about activities
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit first-person statement of the speaker's feelings or evaluation about an activity or experience, use this during extraction to create a preference/state candidate and during CRUD to store it.
content: During extraction: if the speaker explicitly states in first person how an activity or experience makes them feel (e.g., 'it's super exciting and free-feeling'), create exactly one candidate memory as a preference or state; do not infer feelings from third-party or generic statements.

During CRUD: store this candidate as a 'preference' or 'state' memory linked to the activity, with the source message and resolved timestamp; do not merge it into unrelated memories or expand it into additional searches.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that explicit first-person statements of the speaker's feelings or evaluations about an activity or experience are missed during extraction, so durable preference/state memories are never created. This applies to future sessions where a user or role-play speaker directly says how an activity makes them feel (e.g., 'it's super exciting and free-feeling'); it must not apply to third-party statements, inferred emotions, or generic observations without first-person affect.

payload.name: Extract_Explicit_User_Preference
payload.description: When a user explicitly states a favorite or strong preference (e.g., 'X is my favorite', 'Definitely X!'), during extraction, always create a preference candidate even if the message already produced other candidates.
content: During candidate extraction, if a user utterance contains an explicit first-person preference statement naming an item (e.g., 'Definitely X! It's my favorite'), always emit a preference memory candidate for that item, regardless of how many other candidates the message yields.
Do not require the preference to be the message's main topic; a clause or exclamation is sufficient.
Do not apply to hypotheticals, negated statements, or preferences expressed about other people.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction can skip a clearly stated user preference when it appears in a message that already yielded other candidates or when it is phrased as an exclamation. The skill applies to any future session where a user explicitly names an item as their favorite or strongly preferred; it does not apply to implicit likes, negations, or statements about other people's preferences, where the base extraction judgment remains sufficient.

payload.name: Preserve_All_Stated_Preference_Reasons
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly gives multiple distinct reasons or qualities for liking or preferring something, and you are extracting or enriching a profile/preference memory, include every stated reason.
content: During extraction, read the full source message for all explicitly enumerated reasons or qualities attached to a preference (for example, phrases like 'because of X and Y' or 'it is A, B, and C').
Build the candidate content so each distinct stated reason appears; do not keep only the first, most salient, or most recent reason.
Stop after all reasons explicitly present in the message are captured; do not add implied or inferred reasons not stated by the speaker.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes stores only one of several explicitly stated reasons for a preference, leaving later questions about the omitted reason unanswerable. Apply when a message explicitly lists multiple distinct reasons/qualities for the same preference while extracting a profile/preference memory: capture every stated reason. Do not apply when only one reason is stated or other qualities are only implied.

payload.name: Preference-subject attribution from first-person cues
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message expresses a preference or opinion using first-person forms (I, my, love, enjoy) and another participant is mentioned in the session; ensure the memory subject is the speaker, not that other participant.
content: During extraction, if a message uses first-person evaluative forms ('I', 'my', 'I love', 'I enjoy') about a person, team, or thing, set the memory subject to the message's speaker. Do not reassign the subject to another participant only because that person was discussed earlier in the session or appears in the same commit window.

Before ADDing a preference/opinion memory, verify the subject field: if the message states the speaker's own view, the subject must be the speaker. Use a non-speaker subject only when the message explicitly describes that person's preference (e.g., 'Tim loves ...').

If a short reply (e.g., starting with 'Thanks!') continues the speaker's own evaluation, still attribute the memory to the speaker; do not let the addressee or a previously mentioned name override the speaker.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates can misattribute a first-person preference (e.g., 'I love his skills and leadership') to another participant mentioned elsewhere in the same session, creating a memory with the wrong subject. This skill applies when a message contains first-person evaluative cues about a person/team while another entity appears in the conversation context; it requires the memory subject to be the speaker. It does not apply when the message explicitly states a third party's preference.

payload.name: Extract Appreciation from Indirect Statements
payload.description: When a speaker makes an appreciative or positively evaluative statement about a subject, even phrased generally or reflectively, extract a preference/event memory for that speaker during construction.
content: During extraction: if a message contains an explicit appreciative or positively evaluative statement about a subject (e.g., 'Nature truly has a way of reminding us to appreciate the beauty around us'), create a candidate memory (preference or event) recording that the speaker appreciates that subject, even when the statement is not first-person or is phrased as a general reflection.

During CRUD: keep each speaker's appreciation as its own memory; if an appreciation memory for the same subject already exists for another speaker, ADD a separate memory for the current speaker rather than merging or skipping.

candidates.solves: Extraction skips indirect appreciative statements, so a speaker's appreciation is missing from memory. Applies when a speaker makes a reflective/general positive statement about a subject (e.g., nature) that another person has appreciated; record the speaker's own appreciation. Does not apply to messages that only describe a topic without evaluative language or that express someone else's appreciation.

payload.name: Extract attributes from casual ideal-description clauses
payload.description: When a user states an ideal, preferred, dream, or desired version of something in a short, directive, or parenthetical clause, extract each named attribute as a preference memory.
content: Scan every user message for attributes of an ideal, preferred, dream, or desired object even when the sentence is a short directive (e.g., 'Check my ideal X...') or an aside; do not skip the message just because its main intent is a request.
For each distinct attribute stated about that object, create a separate `preference` memory with subject equal to the user, citing the message evidence.
Stop after the attributes explicitly named in the clause; do not infer unstated features or expand into a list of possible preferences.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can skip a user's durable attribute when it is phrased in a short casual or directive clause (e.g., 'check my ideal X by the water') rather than in a full topical sentence, so the preference is never written to memory. The Skill applies when a future message names an ideal, preferred, dream, or desired version of something and lists attributes in terse or parenthetical wording. It does not apply when the user discusses a topic in full sentences, since default extraction already handles that.

payload.name: Extract attributable principle statements as preference memories
payload.description: When a message from an identifiable participant states a general belief, principle, or value judgment (e.g., 'X is the key to Y', 'the best way to ...'), create an extraction candidate for a preference/state memory attributed to that speaker.
content: During candidate extraction, whenever a message contains an explicit general statement from a participant about what is important, key, or best (e.g., 'is the key to', 'is important', 'the best way', 'should always'), create a preference/state candidate that preserves the claim and its speaker attribution.
Require the speaker to be identifiable in the message; do not extract impersonal world knowledge or generic advice that is not tied to a specific participant.
Stop after the principle is captured; do not also extract surrounding encouragement or small talk from the same message.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can silently omit statements where a participant asserts a general belief or principle, leaving no memory for later questions about what that person said. This Skill applies when a future session contains an attributable principle statement (e.g., 'X is the key to Y', 'the best way to ...') made by an identifiable participant, and ensures a candidate is created for a preference/state memory. It should not apply to impersonal world knowledge, pure small talk, or simple first-person preferences that the base extraction already captures.

payload.name: Extract coping and distraction preferences
payload.description: When a session message explicitly links an activity, object, or companion to helping the user cope, distract, or get through tough times, use during extraction to create a preference memory.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that something helps the user through tough times (e.g., 'helps when times get tough', 'nice distraction', 'great company'), create a preference memory for that activity, object, or companion, linked to the source message.
Do not apply to casual mentions of likes or hobbies without a coping or difficult-time context; default extraction handles those. Keep the memory evidence-bound and durable.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes misses explicitly stated coping or distraction preferences, so later questions asking what helps the user go unanswered. This Skill applies when a session message explicitly links an activity, object, or companion to helping the user through difficult times, and requires creating a preference memory for it. It must not apply to ordinary likes or hobby mentions without that coping frame, where the base extraction policy suffices.

payload.name: ExtractPreferenceFromPositiveExclamations
payload.description: When extracting candidates, if a speaker expresses a positive evaluation or exclamation about an object, place, or experience (e.g., 'X is so beautiful!'), create a durable preference memory for that speaker toward the evaluated thing.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit positive evaluative exclamations (e.g., 'so beautiful', 'love it', 'amazing') as evidence of the speaker's durable preference.
Create a `preference` candidate linking the speaker to the object of evaluation only when the statement expresses the speaker's own judgment, not a reported or hypothetical opinion.
Extract at most one preference per distinct evaluated object per message; stop once the preference is captured to avoid redundant candidates.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction fails to generate any candidate when a speaker states a durable preference as an exclamatory positive evaluation (e.g., 'The autumn colors are so beautiful!'), leaving the fact absent from memory. This applies to future sessions where a speaker makes an explicit first-person aesthetic or positive evaluation of an object, place, or experience. It does not apply to reported opinions of others, transient states, or explicit 'I like' statements that the base extraction policy already handles.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitPreferenceStatements
payload.description: When a user explicitly states a personal preference or favorite (e.g., 'I love', 'my favorite is') during extraction, create a preference memory candidate with qualifiers. Use when direct first-person positive preference phrasing appears, even amid other content.
content: During extraction, treat explicit first-person preference statements as mandatory candidates: phrases like 'I love', 'I like', 'my favorite is/are', 'I also love' should each yield a preference memory candidate.
Preserve qualifiers and category context in the candidate (e.g., 'dairy-free chocolate mousse' as a favorite dairy-free treat).
Do not skip a candidate because the message also contains questions or other topics; extract every distinct stated preference.
Do not create candidates from negations ('I don't like'), hypotheticals, or preferences stated about other people; if an identical preference memory already exists, merge/skip instead of duplicating.

candidates.solves: Extraction commonly omits explicit personal preference statements, so no durable memory is created and later questions about the user's favorites fail. Apply when a speaker uses direct first-person positive preference phrasing ('I love X', 'my favorite is X', 'I also love Y') in any message, and create a preference memory candidate, preserving qualifiers like 'dairy-free'. Do not apply to negations, hypotheticals, third-party preferences, or when the same preference memory already exists.

payload.name: Preference extraction from enjoyment statements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states they love, enjoy, or are a big fan of an item or category, extract a `preference` memory capturing what they enjoy, and keep any recommendation in a separate `event` memory.
content: When a message contains an explicit positive affect statement ('I love', 'I enjoy', 'I am a big fan of') about an item or category, extract a `preference` memory for the speaker that states what they enjoy (e.g., enjoying books with adventures and magic), even if the same message also contains a recommendation.
Keep the recommendation, if present, in a separate `event` memory; do not let the event memory replace or absorb the preference statement.
Generalize to the category the speaker enjoys when the loved item exemplifies it (e.g., a book series with adventures and magic means the speaker enjoys those book genres).
Do not apply to messages lacking a stated affect (pure recommendations or actions) or to non-durable one-off states about a specific item.

candidates.solves: Construction agents lose explicit enjoyment when they store a statement like 'I love this series - it has adventures and magic' as only a recommendation event, so later questions about what the speaker enjoys cannot be answered. This Skill applies when a speaker explicitly states love/enjoyment of an item or category; extract a durable `preference` memory capturing that enjoyment and keep any recommendation as a separate `event`. It must not apply to messages that only describe actions (e.g., recommending) without an affect statement, or to one-off states about a single item.

payload.name: Capture preference intensity in media statements
payload.description: During construction extraction, when a speaker expresses strong affinity for a book or media item (e.g., 'favorite', 'really into', 'love'), record it as a preference with that intensity, not merely as a current activity.
content: When extracting from a message, detect explicit preference-intensity language about a book or media item (e.g., 'favorite', 'really into', 'love', 'obsessed with').
Create a preference memory that names the item and reflects the stated intensity (e.g., 'favorite is X' or 'really into X'); do not downgrade it to a neutral activity like 'currently reading'.

Use memory_kind 'preference' only when the statement conveys liking or degree of affinity. If the message only describes what someone is reading or doing without any liking cue, keep it as an event or state memory and do not add intensity.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes loses preference intensity: a statement like 'really into Sapiens' is summarized as 'currently reading', so later queries about favorites fail. This Skill applies when a user expresses strong affinity for a book or other media item using words like favorite, really into, love, or similar. It must not apply to statements that only describe reading or consuming an item without any liking or intensity cue, where the base policy already records a neutral activity or state.

payload.name: Extract explicit self-reported preferences
payload.description: When a participant explicitly states their own preference or favorite (e.g., 'my favorite X is Y', 'I love Z'), create a preference candidate during extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, recognize explicit self-reported preferences: phrases like 'my favorite ... is ...', 'I love ...', 'I enjoy ...', 'I like ...' (positive or negative). Create a `preference` candidate for the speaker, capturing the object and the source message. Do not require extra corroboration; the explicit statement is sufficient.
Do not extract preferences for other people, hypotheticals, or non-preference comments such as 'I have a lot going on'.

candidates.solves: The general problem is that explicit self-reported preferences in conversation are sometimes skipped during candidate extraction, so the fact never reaches memory. Apply in future sessions when a participant says in their own words what they like or dislike (e.g., 'my favorite X is Y', 'I love Z'), and create a preference candidate. Do not apply to hypothetical, negated, or third-party preference statements, which require additional evidence.

payload.name: ExtractUserItemDescriptions
payload.description: When a user shares a photo or link and adds a qualitative description of an owned object, pet, or recent purchase, during extraction create a memory candidate for the description before judging it trivial.
content: During candidate extraction, treat short evaluative statements about the user's own items (e.g., new purchases, pets, home improvements) as memory candidates even when they accompany a photo or casual message.
Extract the description as a preference or state fact only if it conveys a durable quality or opinion the user would want recalled (e.g., 'super cozy and comfy').
Skip statements that are temporary, purely conversational, or not tied to a concrete object the user owns or uses; do not expand one mention into multiple memories.

candidates.solves: General failure mechanism: the construction pipeline skips extraction for user messages that attach a brief qualitative description to an image or link, so durable evaluative facts about owned items are never persisted. Applies to future sessions where a user posts a photo of an object, pet, or purchase and states its qualities in the same message. Does not apply to ordinary statements already covered by base extraction, to purely conversational feedback without a durable object, or to temporary states such as 'it is warm today'.

payload.name: Separate speaker and pet facts during extraction
payload.description: When a user message describes both the speaker and their pet(s)' or animal(s)' distinct reactions, preferences, or behaviors, use separate memory candidates per subject and attribute each fact to the entity that actually experienced it.
content: During extraction, if a message states facts about the speaker and also about their pet(s) or animal(s), create separate candidate memories for each subject instead of merging them into a single profile memory.
Attribute reactions, preferences, and behaviors to the subject that experiences them: the pet's reaction belongs to the pet, the owner's preference belongs to the owner.

During ADD/UPDATE/MERGE, preserve subject-specific facts as distinct memory entries; do not collapse pet and owner facts into one profile memory. Only split the stated facts by subject; do not infer additional facts.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes merges facts about the speaker and their pets into one memory, dropping pet-specific reactions and misattributing preferences, so later questions about the pet cannot be answered. This Skill applies when a future message states distinct reactions, preferences, or behaviors for both the speaker and their pet(s) or animal(s). It does not apply when a message describes only the speaker or only the pet.

payload.name: RecordFamilyPetOwnership
payload.description: When a speaker mentions a pet as belonging to their family or household (e.g., 'my family's dog'), create a state memory of that ownership during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a message includes a possessive reference to a family pet (e.g., 'my family's dog', 'our cat', or a photo caption like 'here's my family's dog'), generate a candidate state memory that the speaker's family has that pet. Include pet type and name if stated.
Do not extract when the pet is hypothetical, explicitly belongs to someone outside the speaker's family, or when the ownership fact is already captured in an existing memory.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage missed an implicit durable fact when a speaker casually mentioned a family pet (e.g., 'here's a photo of my family's dog'), leaving no memory to answer later questions about that speaker's pets. Apply when a future message contains a possessive reference to a pet owned by the speaker's family, from any speaker, to generate a concise state memory with pet type and name if stated.
