Do not apply to hypothetical pets, pets explicitly belonging outside the speaker's family, or passages where the speaker's pet experience is already described explicitly.

payload.name: Extract explicit user relationship statements
payload.description: When a user explicitly states what an entity means to them (e.g., 'feel like family', 'is my best friend'), create a preference or relationship memory candidate before deciding no fact was stated.
content: During extraction, treat first-person statements assigning personal meaning or relationship to an entity (e.g., 'pets feel like family') as durable preference/relationship facts; produce a candidate even if the sentence is phrased with the entity as subject.
Do not extract general world statements (e.g., 'dogs are loyal') or transient opinions (e.g., 'this movie is great') as user memories.

candidates.solves: Extraction often misses memory-worthy facts when a user states a lasting personal view in an indirect phrasing, such as 'pets feel like family', because the subject is the object rather than the user. This Skill applies when a future session contains an explicit statement of how the user values or categorizes an entity and no candidate was extracted, ensuring a preference/relationship memory is written. It must not apply to generic factual claims about the world or one-off opinions that do not express a durable personal relationship.

payload.name: Extract explicit relationship-identity statements during extraction
payload.description: When a user explicitly states how they view someone or something (e.g., 'pets are family', 'she is my best friend'), during construction extraction capture that framing as a profile or relationship memory, even if the message also has activity or photo details.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement of how the speaker views a person, pet, or thing (e.g., 'pets are family', 'she is my best friend'), always create a profile or relationship memory capturing that framing, even when the same message also describes activities or shared photos.

When a later message repeats the same relational framing for an already-known subject (e.g., 'my little family'), prefer confirming/merging into the existing profile memory rather than creating a new activity-only memory.
Stop after capturing the explicit relational claim; do not enumerate every sentiment or opinion in the message.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that explicit self-declarations of relationship or identity framing are omitted when the same message also contains concrete activities or photo-sharing, leaving memories that describe events but not the user's stated view. This skill applies whenever a future message contains a direct statement such as 'X is/are family' or 'I view Y as Z', including repeated references like 'my little family'. It must not apply to messages that only describe activities or photos without an explicit relational claim, where the base extraction is sufficient.

payload.name: PreserveExactObjectNounDuringExtraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory that mentions a gift or object being given or received, use the exact noun the speaker used for that object (e.g., 'pup', not 'stuffed animal'); do not replace it with a different category or an invented item.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly names a concrete object or gift (e.g., 'pup', 'ring', 'book') given or received, record that exact noun in the candidate memory; do not replace it with a different object type, hypernym, or invented item.
If the object is only referenced vaguely (pronoun, metaphor, or no explicit noun), do not guess the object type; either omit it or mark it as unclear based on surrounding evidence.

candidates.solves: General failure: extraction replaces a concrete object noun from the source (e.g., 'pup') with a plausible but incorrect category (e.g., 'stuffed animal'), losing the evidence. Applies when a message explicitly names an object or gift given/received; preserve the literal noun in the memory candidate. Not for messages with ambiguous pronouns or metaphors needing inference.

payload.name: Resolve pronoun antecedents before assigning memory subject
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message that mentions a person and their pets or another group, and later uses 'they'/'them', attribute the claim to the group, not the person; split merged claims by subject.
content: During extraction, identify every entity mentioned in the message (speaker, pets, family, colleagues, etc.) before assigning a memory subject. If the subject of a claim is a pronoun, resolve it to the most recent matching antecedent in the same message; do not default it to the speaker.

When a speaker says their pets (or another group) 'they' do or prefer something, create a separate candidate whose subject is the pets/group, and do not merge that claim with a candidate about the speaker.
If a candidate would combine claims with different subjects, split it so each memory has exactly one subject and remains evidence-bound to the source message.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a message that mentions both a person and their pets (or another group) can yield a single merged candidate where a plural pronoun such as 'they' is misassigned to the person, so the pet's preference is recorded as the owner's. This Skill applies when a future message introduces multiple referents and then uses a plural pronoun that refers to the non-human or non-speaker group; the extractor must resolve the antecedent and keep each subject's claim as its own memory. It does not apply when the pronoun unambiguously refers to the speaker or when only one subject is present.

payload.name: Extract nickname relationships from direct address
payload.description: When a message contains a person being addressed by a nickname, diminutive, or shortened name with the full name identifiable from context, extract a relationship memory for the nickname.
content: During extraction, when a speaker addresses or refers to a person by a nickname or shortened form of the person's name, and the full name is identifiable from the same message, recent context, or existing memory, also create a `relationship` candidate recording that the speaker uses that nickname for the person.
Keep the nickname relationship separate from any event or state candidates in the same message; do not fold it into the event memory.
Do not extract a nickname when the referenced name is the person's full proper name, a title, or an ambiguous placeholder that cannot be confidently linked to a known individual.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction overlooks nickname/alias relationships when a salient event in the same message dominates, leaving 'what nickname' questions unanswerable. This applies to future sessions where a known person is called by a nickname or shortened name and the full name is clearly resolvable, requiring a separate relationship memory. It does not apply to full proper names, titles, or ambiguous terms, where base extraction is already adequate.

payload.name: Extract same-item confirmation replies
payload.description: When a speaker replies to another person's description of a possession or attribute with an explicit confirmation that they also have the same item (e.g., 'I also have...', 'I have one too'), create a candidate memory for that speaker during extraction.
content: During extraction, identify turns where the speaker explicitly confirms possessing the same kind of item or attribute that the previous speaker described (e.g., 'I also have a pendant', 'I have one too', 'me too').

Create a candidate memory for the current speaker (not the previous speaker) recording that they possess that item/attribute; use `state` for a current possession, or `event` when the speaker adds origin or time details.
Do not copy attributes, origins, or symbolic meanings from the previous speaker's description unless the current speaker states them; record only what the current speaker says.
Do not extract when the reply only acknowledges or comments on the other's item without claiming the same item for the speaker (e.g., 'That sounds nice').

candidates.solves: Extraction skips short replies where a speaker confirms they also have an item/attribute just described by another, leaving the speaker's fact unrecorded. Applies during extraction when a turn explicitly claims the same item for the speaker (e.g., 'I also have...', 'I have one too') after another's description; create a candidate for the current speaker. Not for mere acknowledgements or first introductions.

payload.name: Capture-named-comfort-source-during-extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message in which the speaker mentions stress, hardship, or negative feeling alongside a specific named thing that provides cheer, comfort, or joy, ensure the named thing is captured in the extracted memory rather than omitted.
content: During extraction, if an utterance contains both a hardship (e.g., stress, tough competitors, bad day) and a named source of relief or joy (e.g., my turtles, my dog, gardening), extract the source of comfort as its own standalone memory—typically state or preference—stating that the speaker relies on it for cheer and comfort.
Do not replace or swallow the comfort source inside the hardship event; emit both facts: the hardship event (if durable) and the comfort-source relationship.
If the speaker explicitly says the named thing cheers them up, relieves stress, gives joy, or similar, the reliable-referent phrase must be preserved verbatim or near-verbatim in the memory content.
Do not apply when the comfort source is unnamed, generic (e.g., 'things'), or already represented by an existing memory.

candidates.solves: Extraction omits the named comfort source when a speaker mentions both a hardship and something that cheers them up (e.g., "my turtles always cheer me up"), storing only the stress event. Apply when a future session contains both a hardship trigger and a clearly named comforting element; capture the named element as its own memory. Do not apply when no distinct comfort source is named or it is already stored.

payload.name: Extract explicit peace and comfort sources
payload.description: When a user explicitly states that a named activity, object, or place gives them peace, comfort, or helps them cope during grief or difficult times, use this Skill during extraction to create a candidate memory and during CRUD to commit it.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly names a specific activity, object, or place as a source of peace, comfort, or coping during grief or difficult times (e.g., 'X gives me peace', 'X helps me cope'), create one candidate memory for that named source and its context.
During CRUD, commit such candidates as preference or event memories; if an existing memory already covers the same source, use MERGE/UPDATE instead of a duplicate ADD.
Extract at most one candidate per distinct named source per message, and do not extract statements that only express an emotion or mention peace without a named source.

candidates.solves: General failure: extraction skips explicit user statements that name a source of peace, comfort, or coping during grief or difficult times because they look like momentary reactions. Future pattern: a user says 'X gives me peace' or 'X helps me cope/comfort me', and the named source should become a preference or event memory. Boundary: not for emotion-only statements or generic 'I feel at peace' mentions without a named source.

payload.name: Extract Shared Frustration from Explicit Empathy
payload.description: When a user explicitly empathizes with or relates to a frustration previously voiced by another person in the conversation, use during extraction to create a candidate that captures the shared experience for both people.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly says they share, understand, or relate to a frustration that another participant already mentioned in the session, create a candidate recording the shared frustration for both participants (e.g., a state or event with both as subjects), not just the speaker's isolated sentiment.

If an existing memory already captures the other person's individual struggle, create or update a memory that expresses the joint experience (e.g., 'Both X and Y find it frustrating...') rather than duplicating the earlier event.

Do not apply this to simple sympathy without personal alignment, to unrelated complaints about the same topic, or to cases where the speaker merely acknowledges the other's feeling but does not indicate they share it.

candidates.solves: Fixes extraction misses where a speaker's explicit alignment with another person's earlier frustration (e.g., 'I get how frustrating it can be not to find pet-friendly spots') is not recorded as a shared memory, leaving relational facts incomplete. Applies when a speaker expresses they personally share the frustration that another participant has already stated in the session. Does not apply to generic sympathy without stated shared experience, to separate comments about the same topic lacking explicit alignment, or to expanding every mention of a shared topic into a new memory.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitQualifiersInMemoryExtraction
payload.description: During construction, when extracting candidate memories from a message where the speaker explicitly names what they miss, enjoy, or value using a qualitative word (e.g., 'calm', 'fun'), preserve that exact qualifier instead of paraphrasing it as 'the moments'.
content: During candidate extraction, if the source message contains an explicit qualitative or emotional descriptor for an experience the speaker misses, enjoys, or values (e.g., 'calm moments', 'fun times'), keep that descriptor verbatim in the candidate content; do not reduce it to a generic noun like 'the moments'.

When ADD, UPDATE, or MERGE affects an existing memory that already preserves such a stated qualifier, retain that qualifier unless new evidence explicitly contradicts it; avoid later edits silently replacing it with a more general phrase.
Stop once the qualifiers actually present in the source are preserved; do not invent synonyms, add extra adjectives, or expand the memory beyond the speaker's stated wording.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates paraphrase emotional statements and drop the specific qualifier (e.g., 'calm') that later questions target, leaving only a generic noun like 'the moments'. This applies when a speaker's direct speech explicitly names what they miss, enjoy, or value about an activity using a qualitative word, and a memory candidate is being created or updated; preserve that word. It does not apply when the source has no explicit qualifier or when meeting a question would require inferring an unstated one.

payload.name: Extract Figurative Subjective Evaluations
payload.description: When a speaker expresses a feeling, opinion, or evaluation about an activity, object, or experience using figurative, exclamatory, or emphatic language (e.g., 'it's magical!', 'it's a blast!'), and the statement is durable enough to be a memory, extract it as a preference or state during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, treat figurative or exclamatory statements about how an activity, object, or experience feels or matters (e.g., 'it's magical', 'it's a dream') as explicit subjective evaluations. Create a preference or state candidate even without literal 'I feel' or 'I like' phrasing.
Record the underlying evaluation (e.g., the speaker finds the topic magical/joyful) and link it to the specific activity, object, or experience mentioned.

Stop when the exclamation is a transient reaction with no stable subject (e.g., 'wow!') or the figurative phrase does not express a durable feeling/opinion about a specific topic; do not create a candidate in those cases.

candidates.solves: Extraction misses explicit subjective evaluations when phrased figuratively or exclamatorily (e.g., 'it's magical!'), causing durable feelings/opinions to be dropped. Applies when a speaker evaluates an activity, object, or experience in non-literal, emphatic language and the evaluation is stable enough to store as a preference or state memory. Does not apply to literal 'I feel/like' statements, which the base prompt already extracts, nor to transient interjections without a durable subject.

payload.name: Capture explicit feelings during extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a user message, apply this if the speaker explicitly states an emotion or feeling (e.g., 'I feel peace and gratitude') tied to an experience, place, or person.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly states an emotion or feeling about a person, place, or event (e.g., 'I feel so much peace and gratitude'), include that feeling in the candidate content; do not omit it in favor of only situational details.
Limit this to feelings explicitly stated in the message; do not infer or add emotions that were not directly expressed.
Ensure the candidate content can directly answer a future question about how the speaker feels about that experience.

candidates.solves: The failure mechanism is incomplete extraction that drops explicitly stated emotional states from memory candidates. This Skill applies when a user message contains a direct statement of feeling about an experience or relationship and a future question may ask about that feeling. It must not apply when the feeling is only inferred or when the message expresses no explicit emotion.

payload.name: Explicit-Named-Emotion Extraction
payload.description: Use when a message explicitly names emotions a speaker feels about a subject, event, or plan (e.g., relief, excitement, anxiety, worry, hope).
content: When a message explicitly lists emotions a speaker feels about a subject, create or update a `state` memory for that speaker naming each stated emotion and the subject; do not reduce them to 'mixed emotions' or omit them while recording an event or plan.

On later messages that add new named emotions about the same subject, update the existing `state` memory to include the newly stated emotions; keep the subject and the first occurrence's time, and only add emotions that are explicitly stated.
Stop after capturing the explicitly named emotions; do not infer or enumerate additional feelings the speaker did not name.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction tends to record events/plans but drop explicitly named emotions, later collapsing them to 'mixed emotions', so feelings become unanswerable. It applies when a speaker explicitly names emotions (relief, excitement, worry, etc.) about a subject: capture each named emotion in a state memory and update it when new named emotions appear. Not for messages lacking explicit emotion words or using emotions figuratively.

payload.name: Preserve explicit emotion terms in extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a message where the speaker explicitly names their feeling or emotion (e.g., 'I felt joy and freedom'), use this to keep the named emotions exact in the memory content.
content: If the source message explicitly names one or more emotions the speaker felt, preserve each named emotion in the extracted memory content; do not replace any named emotion with a synonym or add an unstated emotion.
Synthesize the rest of the memory from stated facts, but keep the emotion terms exactly as given (e.g., 'joy and freedom' must remain 'joy and freedom', not 'joy and inspiration').
Stop after recording the named emotions and the directly related stated facts; do not expand into inferred feelings or unrelated details.

candidates.solves: During memory extraction, the agent paraphrased a first-person statement of emotion and substituted a named feeling with a similar but different word (e.g., replacing 'freedom' with 'inspiration'), causing the stored memory to fail a later evidence check. This Skill applies to any future session where a speaker explicitly names one or more emotions and the extracted event or state memory must record them faithfully. It does not apply to messages that only imply a mood without naming an emotion, nor to general summarization tasks where no explicit emotion term is at stake.

payload.name: Preserve explicit emotion-linked place details
payload.description: When a user message states a specific place or activity and explicitly links it to a durable feeling or preference such as peace, comfort, or joy, preserve that link as its own memory instead of folding it into a broader thematic summary.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a specific place or activity explicitly said to give the speaker a durable feeling or preference (e.g., peace, comfort, joy), emit a separate candidate recording that specific place-feeling link, even if the message also supports a broader thematic summary.
During CRUD, do not merge or overwrite such a specific place-emotion claim into a broader thematic memory; ADD it as a new memory unless it is already fully captured.

Apply only to concrete, independently queryable claims explicitly tied to an enduring feeling or preference; do not split every clause or create redundant memories for general statements already fully represented.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates can fold a specific place explicitly linked to a durable emotion (e.g., a place the speaker says gives them peace) into a broader thematic summary, hiding the concrete fact from future 'what gives X peace' queries. This Skill applies when a message contains such an explicit place-emotion claim distinct from general narration, and preserves it as its own memory. It must not apply to purely thematic messages or when the claim is already fully captured, to avoid redundant expansion.

payload.name: Capture all explicitly stated emotions in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message where the speaker expresses more than one explicitly stated feeling or attitude about the same subject (e.g., 'discouraged but determined'), include every stated emotion/attitude instead of selecting only one.
content: During extraction, scan the full source message for every explicitly stated emotion, attitude, or sentiment about the subject, including contrasting ones joined by 'but', 'yet', 'although', etc.
Include all found emotions in the candidate content (e.g., 'feels discouraged but determined') rather than omitting any stated feeling.
Stop once every explicitly stated emotion is represented; do not infer or add emotions that are only implied.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often capture only the most salient emotion when a speaker explicitly states mixed or contrasting feelings about the same subject, causing later recall to miss part of the sentiment. This Skill applies whenever a future message contains two or more explicitly stated emotions/attitudes about one topic and the agent is drafting memory candidates. It must not apply to single-emotion statements or to emotions that are only implied, where the base extraction policy already suffices.

payload.name: Capture self-disclosed coping behaviors
payload.description: Use when a speaker explicitly states what they do to relieve stress, comfort themselves, or cope with boredom, such as eating sweets, practicing yoga, or visiting scenic places.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly links a behavior to a purpose such as stress relief, comfort, or relieving boredom (e.g., 'sugary treats are so tempting' in a stress context), create a durable memory (memory_kind 'preference' or 'event') recording the behavior and its purpose; do not capture only the transient emotional state.

During CRUD, when updating a memory that already contains such a behavior-purpose link, preserve the behavioral fact: either keep the behavior in the updated content or retain it as a separate memory while updating only the emotional state.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated behavior; do not infer additional unstated coping activities or exhaustively list every possible stress reliever.

candidates.solves: The general failure mechanism is that extraction omits explicitly self-disclosed coping behaviors, storing only the transient emotional state (e.g., guilt) and losing durable facts about what a person does to relieve stress or comfort themselves. The Skill applies when a future speaker explicitly links an activity to a purpose such as stress relief, comfort, or boredom relief, and such a behavior-purpose relationship is not yet in memory. It must not apply when an activity is mentioned without any self-attributed coping purpose, or when an equivalent memory already exists.

payload.name: Extract explicit emotional reactions to significant events
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit first-person emotional reaction (e.g., 'I felt ...', 'It felt crazy', 'sense of accomplishment') to a notable personal or professional event, before finalizing extraction.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly describes their own emotional reaction to a notable event (signals: 'I felt ...', 'It felt ...', 'sense of accomplishment', 'proud', 'crazy feeling'), create one `state` memory for the feeling with an event context, timestamped from the message.
Anchor the memory to the specific triggering event; do not store emotions that are transient, trivial, or lack a clear event cause.
Link the memory to the source message id; do not add extra searches or unrelated memories.

candidates.solves: The construction extraction stage often skips explicit first-person emotional reactions to significant events (e.g., 'It felt crazy', 'hard work paid off'), leaving future questions about the person's feelings unanswered. This Skill applies when a message directly states a person's emotional reaction to a notable milestone, deal, or life event and should be remembered as a durable state memory. It must not be used for transient small-talk emotions, generic mood updates without an event anchor, or third-party feelings.

payload.name: Preserve ordinal qualifiers in extracted memories
payload.description: During construction extraction, when the source message explicitly identifies an entity by an ordinal or sequential qualifier (first/second/third/last/next), include that qualifier in the extracted memory content so later questions referencing the same ordinal remain answerable.
content: During extraction, if a message states an ordinal or sequential qualifier for an entity (e.g., 'third screenplay', 'second apartment', 'first day'), copy that qualifier into the candidate content rather than paraphrasing the entity generically.

Apply this when the qualifier distinguishes the entity among multiple instances of the same type; if the qualifier is incidental, contextual, or already represented in the memory's subject/relationship, skip it to keep memories compact.
Do not exhaustively list all qualifiers of an entity; only preserve those explicitly needed to answer future ordinal-based identification.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction paraphrases an explicitly numbered entity into a generic noun phrase, so later ordinal-based questions (e.g., 'third screenplay') cannot be answered from memory. This Skill applies when a construction session sees a message naming an entity with an ordinal or sequential qualifier that future queries may reference. It must not apply to incidental descriptors, entities already uniquely identified without the qualifier, or demands for exhaustive qualifier enumeration.

payload.name: Maintain cumulative counts from ordinal milestones
payload.description: When a speaker reports a recurring personal achievement using an ordinal milestone (e.g., 'my fourth tournament win'), extract or update a state memory with the cumulative count and add the new occurrence as a separate event, not an overwrite.
content: Extraction: When a message contains an explicit ordinal milestone (first/second/third/fourth, etc.) for a recurring personal achievement already present in memory, create or update a state memory tracking the cumulative count for that subject and event type (e.g., '<subject> has won N <event type>'), in addition to the individual event candidate.
CRUD: When the new milestone is a distinct occurrence, ADD a new event memory; do not UPDATE or MERGE an earlier event memory to replace its content with the new event, even if the topic matches.
Stop: Maintain the cumulative count only when the ordinal is explicitly stated; do not infer or chain counts from generic mentions such as 'another win' or 'won again'.

candidates.solves: Recurring personal achievements reported with explicit ordinals (first, second, fourth...) are stored only as isolated events and later milestones overwrite earlier ones, so total-count questions fail. Applies when a speaker repeatedly gives ordinal milestones for the same achievement type and a cumulative total may later be queried. Does not apply when the ordinal is not the speaker's own running count or a correct count memory already exists.

payload.name: Preserve-Ordinal-Artifact-Type-in-Event-Extraction
payload.description: When extracting a completion event where the speaker confirms a numbered instance (e.g., 'third one') of a category already established earlier in the session, include the concrete category name and ordinal in the memory instead of a generic label like 'creative project'.
content: During candidate extraction for a completion/achievement event, if the speaker confirms a numbered instance (first/second/third...) of a category that was named earlier in the session, record that concrete category and ordinal in the memory content (e.g., 'completed her third screenplay') rather than a generic label such as 'creative project'. Stop after capturing the confirmed fact; do not add speculation about other works.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes loses the concrete category and ordinal of a newly completed item (e.g., recording 'completed a creative project' when the user confirmed it was the third screenplay), so later count/aggregation queries fail. This Skill applies when a future session contains a confirmation of a numbered instance of a previously mentioned artifact type (e.g., 'Is that your third one?' / 'Yep!'). It does not apply when no ordinal or previously established category is present; there the base extraction policy suffices.

payload.name: Preserve-scope-qualifiers-for-partial-artifacts
payload.description: Use when a user mentions writing, creating, or producing a partial or preliminary version of an artifact (e.g., 'a few bits for a screenplay', 'part of a book', 'draft of a song') during construction extraction or update, especially if an existing memory might refer to the completed artifact.
content: During extraction, preserve scope qualifiers such as 'bits for', 'part of', 'draft of', or 'portion of' in the candidate content; do not upgrade them to the full artifact name (e.g., 'a screenplay') unless the source explicitly states the complete artifact was finished.

During CRUD, before UPDATE or MERGE, compare the candidate's scope with any existing memory about the same artifact. If the candidate is partial or preliminary and the existing memory describes the whole completed item, keep them as distinct memories or add a scope-qualified separate event; do not append the partial event as if it were the same completed artifact.
Stop after applying the qualifier and checking the single most relevant existing memory; do not expand into exhaustive searches or comparisons.

candidates.solves: Extraction and update often collapse qualified partial objects—like 'a few bits for a screenplay'—into the unqualified complete object ('a screenplay'), corrupting later recall, especially when a pre-existing memory already describes the completed full artifact. This Skill applies when a user statement describes a partial, sample, or preliminary version of an artifact and a related existing memory may exist. It must not apply to ordinary summarization where the source unequivocally states completion.

payload.name: Preserve object in product-line memories
payload.description: When a message says someone made/created a limited edition line or collection of a specific item, use during extraction and memory writing to keep the item name instead of writing only 'a line'.
content: During extraction and CRUD, if the source explicitly names the item in a creation/line statement (e.g., 'made a limited edition line of hoodies'), include that item as the object in the candidate and final memory content.
Do not reduce to 'created a limited edition line' when the evidence states what the line was of; keep the concrete noun so later questions about the line's subject can be answered.

candidates.solves: Construction drops the object noun when a person mentions making a line/collection of a specific product, producing memories too generic to answer later 'what did they make a line of?' questions. This Skill applies when extracting statements like 'I made a limited edition line of hoodies' and must record the product type. It does not apply when no product type is stated or the object is already present.

payload.name: Extract explicit hobbies alongside emotional context
payload.description: When extracting candidates from a message that contains both emotional/grief context about a person and an explicit statement of that person's hobby, interest, or passion, ensure the factual attribute is extracted as its own profile candidate in addition to any emotional-state candidate.
content: During extraction: if a message emotionally reflects on a person (e.g., grief, remembrance, missing someone) and also explicitly names a hobby, interest, or passion of that person (e.g., 'reading was one of her hobbies', 'travel was her great passion'), create a separate profile candidate capturing that factual attribute.
Extract each distinct explicitly stated hobby/interest even when they appear in consecutive user messages; do not merge them into an emotional-state memory.
Do not infer hobbies from emotional statements alone; only extract explicit factual statements. If the stated hobby is already present in an existing memory, skip a redundant candidate.

candidates.solves: During candidate extraction, emotional or grief-laden statements about a person can cause explicit factual attributes (hobbies, interests, passions) in the same or adjacent messages to be omitted, losing durable profile information. The Skill applies when a user shares both an emotional reflection about someone and a clearly stated hobby/interest of that person—extract the factual attribute separately. It must not apply when the message only expresses emotion without naming a concrete interest, or when the factual attribute is already captured in existing memories.

payload.name: Preserve evaluative target in extracted memories
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a statement that pairs an emotion or evaluation (e.g., freeing, fun, magical, meaningful) with a specific activity, object, or experience, apply this Skill to keep that target in the candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, if the message contains an evaluative judgment attached to a concrete activity or object, keep both the judgment and its concrete target in the memory content; do not summarize the judgment without saying what it was about.

Stop when the evaluation is only a general description of an experience with no distinct target named in the same utterance; in that case normal extraction rules are sufficient and no additional target is needed.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes keep only a general evaluation (e.g., 'freeing') and drop the concrete target ('dancing and bopping around') it referred to, so later questions about what was evaluated cannot be answered. This Skill applies when a session utterance names both an evaluation and its specific activity or object during memory extraction. It does not apply when the evaluation is only a general description of an experience with no distinct target in the same utterance.

payload.name: Preserve-External-Attribution-During-Extraction
payload.description: When a message states what a class, instructor, course, or organization emphasizes, teaches, or stresses, preserve that entity as the subject of the memory during extraction instead of re-attributing it to the speaker.
content: During extraction, if a message attributes an emphasis, belief, or teaching to an external entity such as a class, instructor, course, or organization, keep that entity as the subject and record the statement as a fact about it; do not convert it into the speaker's own preference or opinion.

Only attribute the statement to the speaker when the speaker explicitly claims it as their own experience or view; otherwise leave the entity mention unchanged so the memory can still answer questions about what that entity emphasizes.

candidates.solves: Constructed memories lose statements about what an external entity (class, instructor, course, organization) emphasizes or teaches because extraction re-attributes the statement to the speaker. Future questions about that entity's teaching become unanswerable. Apply when a message says what such an entity stresses or teaches; do not apply when the speaker is describing their own preference or experience.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitTraitsAndOpinions
payload.description: When a participant explicitly attributes a stable quality or role to another person in praise or evaluation, extract candidate memories for the target's traits and the speaker's relationship.
content: During extraction, treat explicit evaluative statements (e.g., 'Your positivity and determination make you a perfect mentor') as factual candidates: extract a profile memory for the target listing the stated qualities, and a relationship memory from the speaker if the statement reflects the speaker's judgment.
Only extract when the qualities or role are explicitly named; skip generic praise or transient reactions that name no durable attribute.

candidates.solves: The failure occurs when extraction drops explicit statements about a person's stable qualities because they are framed as compliments, so later questions about that trait or opinion return nothing. This applies to any multi-party session where one participant explicitly names another's qualities or role in praise or evaluation; it does not apply to generic praise without a named attribute.

payload.name: Preserve explicit relational experience in extraction candidates
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate from a statement where the speaker explicitly says an activity makes them feel like they are still experiencing it with a specific person, preserve the person, activity, and stated emotional evaluation together.
content: During extraction, if the user explicitly connects an activity to experiencing it with a named person (including a deceased loved one), keep the activity, the named person, and the experience together in the candidate content; do not abstract it to a generic feeling or connection.
Include the user's stated emotional evaluation (e.g., 'hard but comforting') when it is part of the same claim, so the memory can support both the experience and the feeling.
Stop once the candidate contains the explicit relational experience and its evaluation; do not add inferred motives or generalize to other activities.

candidates.solves: Generalizes the extraction failure where a candidate drops the explicit relational object and emotional evaluation of a stated experience, leaving memory unable to answer questions about what the experience means to the speaker. Applies when a future statement describes an activity as feeling like still doing it with a specific person and attaches an emotion; the candidate must preserve person, activity, and emotion. Does not apply to statements that only express general interests or beliefs with no specific relational experience.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitSpeakerValues
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states a value or principle they hold and want to keep in mind for a domain, preserve the exact value, source, and intended application instead of summarizing as a generic discussion.
content: If a message contains an explicit statement of a value/principle the speaker holds or wants to keep in mind (e.g., 'my mom stressed the value of helping others'), extract a memory that records the exact value, the attributed source when named, and the domain of intended application (e.g., engineering projects).
Do not collapse such statements into a generic summary such as 'discussed values' or 'influence of loved ones'; the concrete value must remain directly answerable from memory.
This applies during extraction candidate generation only; do not add extra searches or exhaustive extraction when the value is not explicitly stated in the message.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes over-abstract a speaker's explicit value statement into a generic values discussion, losing the exact fact needed to answer later questions. This Skill applies when a future message contains a speaker-attributed value or principle tied to a domain (e.g., 'my mom stressed the value of helping others for my engineering projects'); it must not apply when a message merely discusses themes without naming a specific value the speaker holds, where a general event summary is sufficient.

payload.name: Extract values from reminder statements
payload.description: When a user says that an object, artwork, quote, or symbol reminds them of or inspires a personal value or behavior, extract that value/behavior as a memory.
content: During extraction, treat messages where the user says something 'is a reminder' or 'reminds me' to uphold a value or behavior: capture the value/behavior as a preference or state memory.
Include the linked object/symbol only if it is useful for future reference, but keep the memory focused on the stated principle, not the object description.
Do not extract when the reminder statement is hypothetical, generic, about someone else, or does not express the user's own durable value.

candidates.solves: Extraction often misses a clear preference when the user expresses it through a symbolic reminder (e.g., 'a painting reminds me to be a leader'), leaving the fact absent from memory. This Skill applies when a future message frames an object, artwork, quote, or symbol as a reminder or inspiration for the user's own personal value or behavior; it should extract that value/behavior as a durable memory. It must not apply to statements that merely describe a decorative object or a trait with no stated personal significance, nor to hypothetical, generic, or third-party statements.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitOutcomesInExtraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a statement in which someone helped, mentored, or supported others and the statement explicitly names an achieved outcome or goal (e.g., 'reach their goals'), preserve that concrete outcome in the memory content instead of paraphrasing it away.
content: During extraction, identify explicit outcomes, achievements, or goals reached that the speaker attributes to someone's help or mentoring (e.g., 'develop and reach their goals').
Include those concrete outcomes verbatim or near-verbatim in the extracted memory content; do not replace them with generic summaries such as 'growth and development' that lose the specific result.
Do not infer outcomes that are not explicitly stated; if no concrete goal is mentioned, continue with the normal compact summary.

candidates.solves: The general failure is extraction summarization dropping explicit outcomes or goals from raw evidence, leaving memories that only imply help. This skill applies when a future session contains a statement about helping, mentoring, or supporting others that names a concrete achieved result (e.g., 'reach their goals') and that result must be captured as a durable fact. It must not apply when no specific outcome is stated, where the normal compact paraphrase remains sufficient.

payload.name: Preserve stated attributes of recommendations
payload.description: When a speaker recommends or mentions an item with an explicitly stated attribute or reason, use this during extraction and CRUD to keep that qualifier in the memory candidate and in the stored memory.
content: During extraction, if the source states a recommendation together with an explicit attribute or reason (e.g., 'X is calming and cute', 'Y is great for beginners'), record that qualifier as part of the candidate content instead of reducing the item to a bare name in a list.

During UPDATE or MERGE, when an existing memory already covers the recommended item, merge the stated attribute onto that item and keep the evidence link; do not overwrite the memory with a summary that omits the attribute.
Only preserve qualifiers the speaker explicitly linked to the item; do not add inferred attributes, and do not list every adjective when the speaker did not attach it to the recommendation.

candidates.solves: Construction summarization often drops explicitly stated attributes or reasons attached to a recommended item, so later questions about that attribute fail. This Skill applies when a speaker pairs a recommendation with a stated qualifier (e.g., 'calming and cute', 'great for beginners') and the extraction candidate would otherwise list the item without that qualifier. It does not apply when no attribute is stated or when the attribute is inferred rather than explicitly spoken by the speaker.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Belief Statements in Dialogue
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly tells another person a belief, attitude, or principle that the person should adopt or remember, use during extraction to create a memory capturing that stated claim.
content: During extraction, treat as a candidate any message where one participant explicitly frames a belief/attitude/principle for another, e.g., 'remember that X', 'it's important for you to believe X', 'you should know X', 'your X is not defined by Y'. Preserve the framed proposition X as the memory text; it is a durable claim, not filler.

Create an `event` memory recording that the speaker told the addressee this belief, or a `state` memory for the belief/attitude itself; link it to the source message. Use whichever kind matches how the memory will be retrieved.

Do not apply to generic encouragement without a proposition ('you can do it', 'I know it's hard') or to passing factual statements about third parties. Apply only when the speaker assigns a specific belief/principle to the addressee.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction failures where an explicit belief/attitude statement is embedded in supportive dialogue and never becomes a memory candidate. It applies when one participant tells another a specific belief or principle they should hold, phrased as important to believe or remember. It must not apply to generic encouragement without a concrete proposition or to factual statements about third parties.

payload.name: Preserve Evaluation Descriptors in Memory Extraction
payload.description: Use during construction when a speaker's statement contains both an overall evaluation and specific sensory/qualitative descriptors, so the extracted memory keeps both instead of only the verdict.
content: During extraction, if a message gives an overall evaluation (e.g., 'delicious', 'super good') plus explicit descriptors (e.g., 'rich and creamy', 'too spicy'), include both the verdict and those descriptors in the candidate content; do not compress the qualifiers away.
Stop after the explicitly stated descriptors; do not infer additional traits or expand the memory.
During CRUD, if an existing memory has the verdict but lacks an explicitly stated descriptor found in the source message, update/merge to add that descriptor; otherwise do not modify.

candidates.solves: When extraction summarizes an evaluative statement, it can keep only the verdict and drop explicit qualifiers, making later questions about those qualities unanswerable. Applies whenever a message gives both a global evaluation (e.g., delicious, super good) and concrete descriptors (e.g., rich and creamy) of an experienced thing. Does not apply when no qualifiers exist, qualifiers are transient physical states, or existing memory already preserves both.

payload.name: Extract explicit motivation statements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states what motivates them or their team to improve (e.g., 'X drives us to get better', 'what motivates us is X'), use this during extraction to create a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly names a motivator for themselves or their own team (phrases like 'X drives us to...', 'what motivates us is X', 'X pushes us'), create a compact memory (state or preference) with the motivator as the object, linked to the speaker and source message.
Only extract when the motivation is stated explicitly by the speaker; do not infer motivation from actions, events, or third-party descriptions.

candidates.solves: The failure is that explicit self-reported motivation facts are skipped during extraction, so later questions about what motivates a speaker or their team have no memory to retrieve. This applies when a speaker directly names the trigger for their own or their team's improvement (e.g., 'that's what drives us to get better'). It must not apply where motivation is only implied or when the message is a plain event narrative.

payload.name: Preserve Exact Descriptive Adjectives in Memory Extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a message where a speaker directly describes a person, place, or thing with a specific evaluative adjective or short descriptive phrase, preserve that exact term in the candidate content instead of replacing it with a general sentiment label.
content: During extraction, when a speaker directly describes a person, place, or thing with a specific evaluative adjective or short descriptive phrase, preserve that exact term in the candidate content; do not replace it with a general sentiment label.
When the candidate updates an existing memory about that entity or relationship, include the descriptor in the new content if it is not already present; skip only if the exact term is already stored.

candidates.solves: When a speaker directly characterizes an entity with a specific evaluative adjective or short descriptive phrase, extraction often paraphrases it into a general sentiment, so later questions about the exact description cannot be answered from memory. This Skill applies when creating or updating a memory from a message containing such a direct characterization and the descriptor is the factual content to preserve. It does not apply when the descriptor is already stored, when only an implied feeling appears without a specific term, or when the descriptor is incidental to the memory's purpose.

payload.name: Preserve specific facts when paraphrasing extraction candidates
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate during construction, and the user states a concrete function, role, or mechanism of a device, person, or activity, keep that exact detail in the candidate content rather than collapsing it into a generic paraphrase.
content: During extraction, when paraphrasing a user statement into a candidate, preserve every specific factual detail the user states (concrete functions, roles, mechanisms, and named relationships); do not replace them with generic labels like 'motivated' or 'healthy' unless the source itself is that generic.
If a user statement contains multiple distinct concrete facts about the same subject, include each fact in the candidate; do not merge or broaden them in a way that omits one.
Do not expand beyond the source: only keep details the user actually states, and stop once all substantive facts are captured in the candidate.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes paraphrase a user's concrete factual statement into a generic one (e.g., replacing 'serves as a constant reminder to keep going' with 'stay motivated'), silently dropping evidence needed to answer later questions. This Skill applies when a user names a specific function, role, or mechanism of an object or person and the extracted candidate risks losing that detail; it does not apply when the paraphrase already preserves all substantive facts or when the source statement itself is generic.

payload.name: Preserve explicit metaphors in relationship extraction
payload.description: When extracting a relationship or shared-experience memory from a message where a speaker uses a concrete metaphor or analogy (e.g., 'like having a partner to dance with'), include the comparison itself in the candidate content, not only the inferred support or encouragement.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly compares a relationship or shared endeavor to a concrete image, preserve that comparison in the memory content alongside any inferred support or emotional meaning.
Do not summarize the metaphor away as only 'support each other' or 'encourage one another'; keep the literal comparison so later questions about how they described it remain answerable.
When updating an existing relationship memory, enrich it with the comparison instead of replacing prior supportive details, and retain both the concrete description and the supportive meaning.

candidates.solves: During extraction, figurative comparisons in conversation are often reduced to their inferred emotional meaning, so the concrete analogy is lost and later questions about what someone compared something to cannot be answered from memory. This Skill applies when a speaker explicitly uses a metaphor or analogy to characterize a relationship, shared experience, or journey and the memory should retain that comparison. It does not apply to ordinary supportive statements without an explicit comparison or to throwaway idioms that do not describe the relationship.

payload.name: Extract Durable Object Significance
payload.description: When a user states what an object, photo, place, or keepsake reminds them of or means to them, and this is a durable sentiment, use during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a user says an object/photo/place/keepsake reminds them of, symbolizes, or has lasting meaning (e.g., 'reminds me of...', 'symbolizes...', 'means a lot because...'), create a candidate memory capturing that durable sentiment, linked to the item.
Apply only when the sentiment is stable and identity-relevant; skip transient emotional states and purely factual descriptions of the object.
Link the memory to the source message and resolve relative time from the session timestamp.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often fails to capture explicit user statements of personal meaning or sentiment toward an object, so durable facts are never stored. This Skill applies when a future user says an object, photo, place, or keepsake reminds them of or symbolizes a lasting feeling or relationship; extract a memory. It must not apply to transient moods, simple factual descriptions of the item, or one-time remarks without enduring significance.

payload.name: Preserve specific wording and exclude unsupported details in memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate from a user message, use this if the source contains a concrete phrase, object, or entity that is central to the fact, to avoid generalizing it away or adding unstated details.
content: When composing a memory candidate, keep the source's specific wording for the core fact; do not replace a concrete phrase with a vaguer synonym (e.g., turn 'savor all the good vibes' into 'savor the moment') unless the paraphrase is fully equivalent in meaning.
Do not introduce entities, people, times, or locations that are not explicitly stated in the source message; treat reasonable-sounding assumptions as unsupported and exclude them from the memory.
If the source message asserts several distinct facts, extract them as separate memory candidates rather than merging them with inferred context.

candidates.solves: General mechanism: extraction candidates paraphrase specific source claims into vaguer or altered facts, and add unmentioned entities, producing memories that lose the ground truth. Applies when creating any memory candidate from a message that states a specific action, object, or event detail; require preserving the source's exact core wording and omitting unstated entities. Does not apply when the paraphrase preserves the factual content equally or when the message lacks the specific detail.

payload.name: Preserve exact descriptive wording in memories
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly describes a subject with a specific word or short phrase (e.g., 'awesome', 'difficult'), preserve that exact term when extracting or updating memories; do not substitute a synonymous paraphrase.
content: During extraction, if the source message contains an explicit description or evaluation of a subject, keep the speaker's exact descriptive term in the memory content; do not replace it with a synonym (e.g., 'awesome' must not become 'strong').
During CRUD, when updating or enriching an existing memory, retain any exact descriptive term that came from a source unless a newer source explicitly changes it.
Apply only to direct descriptive statements where the wording itself is the fact; for general narrative summaries, paraphrasing for compactness remains acceptable.

candidates.solves: Paraphrasing an explicit evaluative term during extraction silently changes the stored fact (e.g., 'awesome' becomes 'strong'), making later questions about how something was described unanswerable. This Skill applies when a source message states a specific description or evaluation of a subject and a memory is created or updated from it. It does not apply to compressing longer narratives, where the exact wording is not a distinct claim.

payload.name: Preserve explicit activities when extracting event memories
payload.description: During memory extraction, use when a user message about an event contains both an explicit activity/action and emotional or qualitative descriptions; ensure the concrete activity is captured as a factual part of the candidate memory.
content: When extracting an event memory, explicitly named activities or actions (e.g., dancing, hiking, cooking) are factual content that must be preserved; do not let emotional or qualitative descriptors like 'freeing', 'magical', or 'great' replace them.

If a message states both what the speaker did and how they felt about it, include the concrete action in the candidate memory even when the message also contains strong subjective language; a summary that only records the emotion is incomplete.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes drops explicitly stated activities while preserving emotional or qualitative language, leaving event memories incomplete. This Skill applies when building an event memory from a user message that pairs a concrete action (e.g., dancing, hiking, cooking) with feelings or opinions about it. It does not apply when the message contains no explicit activity, or when the activity is already captured in the candidate.

payload.name: Include explicit reasons in event candidates
payload.description: When extracting an event or state-change candidate and the message states the reason for it, include that reason in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a message states an action or event and also gives the reason for it (e.g., 'I got X because I saw Y'), encode the reason in the same event memory content.
Only include reasons that are explicitly stated in the message; never infer or add motivations absent from the source.

candidates.solves: Extraction often captures the fact of an event or state change but drops the reason explicitly stated in the same message, so later 'why' questions cannot be answered from memory. This applies when a future message reports an event/state change together with its reason (e.g., 'I got X because I saw Y'); the event memory should include that reason. It must not apply when no reason is stated, since inferring motivation would introduce unsupported facts.

payload.name: Preserve explicit gift events over abstract summaries
payload.description: When a message states a concrete past event (e.g., someone gave/received a specific object at a stated age/time) and also adds commentary about its significance, extract the concrete event as a memory and do not let the commentary replace it.
content: During extraction, if an utterance contains an explicit event like 'X gave me Y when I was Z' or 'I got Y at age Z', extract a memory that names the giver, the object, and the age/time, even when the sentence also includes commentary such as 'it was the start of my passion'.
Do not fold the concrete event into a broader summary or omit the object; if the commentary is durable too, record it as a separate memory, but never lose the giver-object-time fact.

candidates.solves: This addresses a construction failure where an utterance states a concrete past event (someone gave the speaker a specific object at a stated age) together with commentary about its significance, but the extraction candidate records only the abstract consequence and loses the concrete event. It applies when a future session message contains an explicit gift/event with giver, object, and age/time alongside such commentary. It does not apply when the message only describes an interest, hobby, or support without mentioning a concrete object being given or received.

payload.name: Preserve explicit process descriptions in event extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory and the speaker explicitly describes the process or manner of an action with specific phrases, include that explicit description in the candidate content.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement of how or in what manner an action was performed (e.g., 'embracing the creative process without restraint'), preserve that phrase or its close paraphrase in the candidate memory content; do not replace it with only a general summary of emotions or outcomes.
If the message only provides emotional reactions, descriptions, or outcomes without an explicit process/manner statement, keep the existing summarization approach.

candidates.solves: General failure: extraction candidates drop explicit process/manner phrases from user statements, summarizing only emotions or outcomes, so later queries about how something was done cannot be answered. Applies to future sessions where a user explicitly describes how they created or performed something (for example, painting, cooking, writing) and that manner is part of the durable event. Does not apply when the user only states emotions, results, or descriptions without any explicit process statement.

payload.name: Preserve stated decision reasons in extraction
payload.description: When a message states a decision (chose, decided, got, picked) with an explicit reason in the same utterance ('because', 'since', 'felt like', 'was fascinated'), extract the reason into the memory content so future 'why' questions are answerable.
content: If a message pairs a decision or choice with an explicit reason (e.g., 'because', 'since', 'felt like', 'was fascinated by'), include that causal explanation in the same memory content instead of only recording the outcome or its later benefits.
During extraction, keep the reason compactly attached to the decision (e.g., 'chose X because Y'), preserving the link; do not drop the motivation clause when summarizing the event or preference.
Do not infer or add a reason when none is stated, and skip the reason if it is already present in an existing or simultaneous memory.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction preserves the outcome of a decision but drops the explicitly stated motivation, so later 'why did X...' questions lack evidence. The Skill applies when a future message states a choice together with an explicit reason in the same utterance and that reason is not yet in memory. It must not apply when no reason is given (inferring one would be unsupported) or when the reason already exists in another memory.

payload.name: Extract self-taught skill claims as distinct memories
payload.description: When a message explicitly states that a person taught themselves a skill, learned on their own, or is self-taught, extract that fact as its own memory even if the same message also mentions other people's support or involvement.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement that the speaker (or subject) taught themselves a skill, learned on their own, or is self-taught, create a separate durable event memory capturing that self-learning fact.

Do not fold the self-taught claim into a broader memory about interest, passion, or family support; it must be preserved as a standalone claim so questions about how the person learned remain answerable.
Other context in the same message (e.g., supportive parents) may be extracted separately, but the self-taught fact must not be omitted or merged away.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes merge several explicit claims from one message into a single event memory and silently drop the claim about how a skill was acquired, especially self-taught statements such as 'I taught myself' or 'learned on my own'. This will recur in conversations where a speaker states self-instruction while also mentioning supportive context like family encouragement. The Skill must not apply when learning was done with others' help or self-teaching is only implied, because base extraction already covers ordinary event extraction.

payload.name: Preserve explicit origin events during extraction
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message narrates how a person started, was introduced to, or began a long-term activity or relationship, especially when the message also contains surrounding context.
content: When extracting from a narrative that states an origin (e.g., 'dad signed me up for a local league'), include the explicit initiating event as a distinct clause in the memory; do not let surrounding context (e.g., 'I would watch NBA games with my dad') replace it.
Preserve the actor, action, and object of the origin statement, then stop; do not expand the memory with every detail in the narrative.
Do not infer an origin when the message only describes ongoing activity without an explicit starting event.

candidates.solves: Extraction drops the explicit origin event when condensing a narrative, so memories cannot answer how an activity began. Applies whenever a single message states how someone started or was introduced to a long-term activity and that initiating event must be kept. Not for messages that only describe ongoing involvement with no stated origin.

payload.name: IncludeExplicitPlanItemsInEventMemories
payload.description: When extracting an event or plan memory from a conversation where participants explicitly name activities, items, or things they will try, include those exact details in the memory content instead of summarizing them with a generic label.
content: When composing or updating an event/plan memory, scan the related messages for explicitly stated activities, items, or things the participants plan to try (e.g., 'try fresh pastries', 'grab coffee'). Include each explicit detail in the memory content; do not replace them with a general label such as 'coffee date' or 'meet up'. Stop at the explicit details—do not infer unmentioned activities or items. If a later message contradicts or supersedes an explicit detail, update the memory to reflect the change.

candidates.solves: Extraction often collapses an explicitly described plan into a generic label (e.g., 'coffee date') and drops named activities such as 'fresh pastries', making them unrecoverable when answering later questions. This applies when a future conversation states a plan/event with specific activities or items across one or more messages and a candidate memory is being composed or updated. It must not apply when no explicit activities are named or when including details would require inference beyond the text.

payload.name: Extract Explicit User State Statements
payload.description: During extraction, when the user explicitly states a current personal condition or situation they are dealing with (e.g., 'dealing with work stress'), create a state or event memory for it.
content: During extraction, if the user explicitly names a current personal condition or experience (e.g., 'dealing with X', 'feeling Y'), extract it as a state memory (or event if time-bound) even if it appears in a casual or multi-topic message.
Resolve relative time from the message/session timestamp; if the condition is explicitly time-bound, record it as an event; otherwise record as state.
Do not extract when the statement is hypothetical, about another person, or a general remark not describing the user's own current situation.

candidates.solves: Extraction may omit explicit user statements about their current state, leaving memory incomplete for later questions. This Skill applies when a user directly says what they are dealing with or experiencing (e.g., 'dealing with work stress'); require creating a state or event memory with resolved time. It must not apply to hypothetical statements, third-party remarks, or generic commentary already covered by base extraction.

payload.name: Extract Concrete Event When a Reply Names a Photo Activity
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message references an activity indirectly (e.g., a photo or vague 'cooking a meal') and a follow-up message in the same session explicitly identifies the concrete result; extract the specific event memory instead of only a general preference.
content: During extraction, process both the speaker's indirect message and the immediate reply that names the concrete activity; do not skip the reply.

If a message shows or describes an activity without naming its specific result, and another participant then identifies the result explicitly (e.g., 'That slow cooker meal looks yum!'), add an event memory stating that the speaker performed the named concrete activity, with the reply message as evidence.
Do not add speculative dish or result names when no message names them, and do not expand from one named example to other unmentioned activities.

candidates.solves: This addresses extraction-stage omissions where a concrete event is only recoverable from the combination of an indirect/media message and a follow-up reply that names the activity. Applies when a speaker shares a photo or indirect description of doing something and the next message explicitly identifies the specific item or result, so the memory should record that concrete event. Does not apply when the activity is fully stated in a single message, when the reply is only praise or opinion without naming a concrete result, or when the evidence remains ambiguous.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated components of a single claim
payload.description: When a user message explicitly lists multiple distinct components describing the same subject or claim (e.g., themes of a work, traits of a person, items in a plan), use this during candidate extraction to keep every listed component in the memory instead of dropping any.
content: During extraction, if the source message explicitly enumerates multiple components of the same subject or claim (e.g., 'about X, Y, and Z', 'has A, B, and C'), include all of the enumerated components in the candidate memory content; omitting any listed component is an error.

Apply this only to components that are presented as a deliberate list belonging to one claim. Do not pad memories with unrelated or incidental details, and stop once every explicitly stated distinct component is captured.

candidates.solves: During extraction, a candidate memory can silently drop one item from an explicitly enumerated set of components that form a single claim (e.g., a movie described as being about X, Y, and Z), so a later question about the missing component fails. This Skill applies when a future message lists multiple distinct components of one fact and the extractor must choose what to include: preserve every enumerated component in the memory content. It must not apply to non-enumerated background detail or to forcing exhaustive coverage of every incidental topic, which would bloat memories.

payload.name: Preserve all distinct stated attributes in extraction
payload.description: Use when extracting a memory candidate from a user message that states multiple distinct attributes or evaluations about the same event or entity, to ensure all explicitly stated attributes are kept in the memory.
content: During extraction, when a single user message states multiple distinct facts or opinions about the same subject (e.g., a movie's storyline and its acting), include every explicitly stated attribute in the candidate content, either in one concise sentence or as separate candidates.
Do not collapse to one attribute or add unsupported details; omit only non-factual filler such as time adverbs ('the other day') or emphasis words.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage sometimes keeps only one of several distinct attributes a user states about the same event (e.g., a movie's story vs. its acting), so later questions about the dropped fact cannot be answered. Applies when a single user message explicitly states multiple attributes of the same referent and a candidate memory is being created; the candidate must preserve all distinct stated facts. Does not apply when the omitted detail is not a distinct factual claim (filler, timing) or is already captured elsewhere.

payload.name: ExtractDistinctClaimsFromMultiClaimMessages
payload.description: When a message contains several distinct durable statements about the user's experiences or preferences, extract each as its own candidate instead of keeping only the most salient one.
content: During extraction, if a message states multiple distinct durable facts (e.g., 'time with X is valuable' and 'time with Y is relaxing'), create a separate candidate for each fact rather than selecting only one.
Never drop a claim solely because another seems more salient; every distinct preference/experience statement in the message is evidence-bound and should be preserved.
Stop when each distinct claim has its own candidate; do not split a single claim into multiple paraphrases or extract non-durable small talk.

candidates.solves: Extraction frequently preserves only the most salient preference from a multi-part message, so later answers miss other supported claims. Apply when a single message contains multiple distinct durable statements about the user's experiences or preferences (for example, one activity described as valuable and another as relaxing) and each deserves its own memory candidate. Do not apply to single-claim messages or to splitting one claim into redundant paraphrases.

payload.name: Split multi-fact messages into separate candidates
payload.description: During extraction, when a single message reports both an emotional reaction/state about an event and a separate plan or goal, create separate candidates for each instead of merging only one fact into an existing memory update.
content: If a message expresses a subjective reaction or emotional state about something that happened AND a distinct plan, goal, or ongoing focus, emit at least two separate candidates: one event/state candidate for the reaction and one plan candidate for the goal.
Do not merge such a mixed message into a single UPDATE of an existing memory unless the updated content preserves both facts; otherwise the dropped fact becomes unrecoverable.
Stop after separating the distinct fact types in the message; do not enumerate every minor detail or create redundant candidates.

candidates.solves: Extraction loses a memory fact when one message states both an emotional reaction to an event and a separate plan or goal, because the candidate captures only the plan and updates an existing memory, dropping the reaction. Applies to future sessions where a speaker reports a feeling about an event plus current plans in the same message. Does not apply to messages that express a single fact or where the existing candidate already preserves all stated facts.

payload.name: Extract-All-Enumerated-Profile-Items
payload.description: When a user message lists multiple hobbies, interests, or preferences for the same person, extract each listed item into one candidate and merge it into the existing profile memory rather than recording only the first or most emphasized item.
content: If a single user turn enumerates several hobbies, interests, or preferences of the same subject, include every listed item in the extracted candidate; do not select only the first or most elaborated one.

Before adding a new memory for one of these items, check the retrieved existing-memory pool for a profile memory of the same subject; if one exists, create a candidate that merges the new items into it so the complete enumerated list is preserved.
Stop enumerating once the message no longer explicitly lists another item; do not infer additional hobbies beyond what the speaker states.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often capture only one item from a message that enumerates multiple hobbies or preferences, so later items are never memorized. This applies when a user lists two or more durable interests for the same person in one turn and a profile memory for that person exists; merge all listed items into that memory. Do not use when the message states a single activity or a non-durable event.

payload.name: Extract co-occurring durable facts during extraction
payload.description: Use during candidate extraction when a single message contains both an immediate action and a separate durable fact about the same person, such as starting or owning a business, to ensure both are captured as distinct memories.
content: When a message states both a current action (e.g., launching a campaign, expanding) and a separate durable fact about the same person (e.g., 'Starting my own store...', 'I own...'), create one candidate for each distinct fact; do not let the more salient action suppress the other fact.

Before finalizing extraction candidates, re-read the message for explicit statements of ownership, creation, or career decisions, and add them as separate candidates even when they support an action already captured.
Only extract the durable fact when the text explicitly states or clearly implies it (e.g., 'my own store' plus 'starting' implies ownership); do not infer unstated facts.

candidates.solves: Construction fails when extraction from a multi-fact message keeps only the salient action (e.g., launching an ad campaign) and drops a separately stated durable fact (e.g., starting one's own store), leaving memory unable to answer later questions about that state.
