This Skill applies to any future message where a speaker explicitly states or clearly implies a lasting decision or state alongside a concrete action, so both yield separate candidates. It does not apply when the message contains only one durable fact, or when the alleged state is merely inferred without textual support.

payload.name: Preserve distinct items in listed advice
payload.description: When a source message enumerates multiple distinct pieces of advice, instructions, or facts (separated by 'and', commas, or bullets), preserve each separate item in the memory content instead of collapsing them into one umbrella phrase.
content: During extraction, if a message lists separate actionable points (e.g., 'slowly and gently, paying attention to...' plus 'stay patient and positive'), write candidate content that includes each distinct point; do not replace them with a single broad phrase like 'emphasizing patience and gentleness' that can drop specifics such as 'slowly' or 'positive'.

Merge items only when they are synonymous or redundant; if a future question could ask for any listed item, keep it in the memory. When reviewing candidates during CRUD, if an added memory dropped an item from an enumerated source, update it to restore the missing detail.

candidates.solves: Extraction summaries of multi-part advice often collapse separate recommendations into a general theme, dropping specifics that later questions need. This Skill applies when a message explicitly lists two or more distinct instructions or facts and a candidate summarizes them under one umbrella term; it tells the Constructor to preserve each distinct item and only merge true synonyms. It does not apply to single-idea messages or redundant restatements, where compact summarization is already correct.

payload.name: ExtractEachDistinctStatement
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a single message contains multiple distinct statements—such as a plan or invitation plus a separate intention or hypothetical activity—and each needs its own memory candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, emit a separate candidate for each distinct durable fact in a message. If a message states both a concrete plan/invitation and a separate personal intention or hypothetical activity (e.g., a joke about pursuing a creative project), create one candidate for each rather than only the most prominent fact. Stop when every distinct fact is covered; do not split rephrasings, elaborations, or supporting details of the same fact.

candidates.solves: Extraction drops a secondary durable fact when a message already yields a more prominent one, leaving memory incomplete. Apply when a single message states both a plan/invitation and a separate intention or hypothetical activity (e.g., a joke about a future creative project); emit a separate candidate for each. Do not apply when the secondary text only elaborates the primary fact or when only one distinct fact exists.

payload.name: Preserve distinct stated impacts during memory extraction
payload.description: When extracting or updating a memory from a message where the speaker states multiple distinct impacts, reactions, or takeaways, apply this Skill to keep each explicit concept instead of merging them into one paraphrase.
content: During candidate extraction and when updating an existing memory, compare the candidate against the source message for explicitly stated distinct impacts, effects, or takeaways.
If the speaker names more than one distinct concept, preserve each one as its own clause or as a separate candidate; do not let one paraphrase subsume another.
Use the speaker's own named terms where possible, and stop once every explicitly stated distinct concept is represented; do not add inferred or exhaustive extra detail.

candidates.solves: The general failure is extraction paraphrase loss: when a user's message names several distinct impacts, effects, or takeaways, the candidate memory merges them and drops one, so later questions about the omitted concept cannot be answered. This Skill applies when constructing or updating memories from any statement listing more than one explicit reaction, impact, or thematic takeaway, and instructs preserving each stated concept. It does not apply to single-concept statements or to adding inferred detail not explicitly named.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated items in extraction
payload.description: Use when extracting a memory from a user message that enumerates multiple distinct items sharing one common attribute or sentiment, such as what made an experience relaxing, enjoyable, or notable.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a list of items tied to a single shared predicate (e.g., 'fresh air, peacefulness, and a cozy cabin made it a retreat'), include every listed item in the candidate content; do not paraphrase away any member of the list.
If the list is long, keep all items in one concise memory rather than omitting members; only omit items that are clearly illustrative examples the user does not intend as complete.
Do not apply this to messages without an enumeration of distinct items; a single descriptive phrase can be summarized normally.

candidates.solves: When a user message lists several items that all share the same attribute or experience (e.g., what made a trip relaxing), candidate extraction sometimes captures only a subset, so the stored memory omits valid evidence. This skill ensures every enumerated item is preserved in the extracted candidate during construction. It should not apply to messages that do not contain a genuine list of distinct items, or when the user frames the list as non-exhaustive examples; those cases should remain compact.

payload.name: ExtractEachDistinctActivityFromList
payload.description: When a user message describes multiple distinct ongoing activities or interests (e.g., writing about X, studying Y, making recommendations Z), apply during extraction to capture each distinct activity as a separate memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message lists two or more distinct ongoing activities or recurring practices (connected by 'and', commas, or as a list), generate a separate ADD candidate for each distinct activity that is not already fully captured by an existing memory or by another candidate in the current batch.
Do not skip a message merely because its topic resembles an earlier message; verify that every distinct activity named in the current message is represented in the candidate set before proceeding.
Stop after each distinct activity is captured once; do not create separate memories for paraphrases that restate the same activity.

candidates.solves: Construction fails when a user message enumerates several distinct ongoing activities or practices and extraction retains only the most salient one, losing the rest. This Skill applies to any session where a single message lists multiple distinct ongoing activities or interests (e.g., writing about X, studying Y, making recommendations Z) that warrant durable memory, and it should not be used for one-off events already fully captured or for paraphrases of the same fact.

payload.name: Preserve-All-Listed-Facts-In-Extraction
payload.description: When composing memory content from a message that lists multiple distinct facts about one subject, use if the list items are separated by 'and', commas, or separate sentences, and ensure every distinct fact is included instead of paraphrasing a subset.
content: When composing memory content from a message, identify all distinct facts about the subject, especially items joined by 'and', commas, or separate sentences. Include every distinct fact in the candidate or updated memory content.
If a full enumeration would make one candidate too long or mix different memory kinds, create separate candidates for each distinct fact instead of dropping any.
Do not paraphrase a subset: if the source says 'shared worries and hopes', keep both; if it lists several activities, keep all.
Stop enumerating when the message is only general background, restates the same fact, or uses vague language with no separate concrete items.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes summarize a detailed statement and drop one of several enumerated facts (e.g., recording only some items from an 'and' list), leaving the memory partially covering the source. This Skill applies when a future message about one subject contains multiple distinct facts and the agent writes a candidate or updated memory from it; the closest non-case is a message with repetitive restatements or general background, where no additional enumeration is required.

payload.name: Preserve all explicitly listed preference traits
payload.description: Use when extracting or updating a preference/admiration memory from a message that explicitly lists multiple distinct qualities, traits, or reasons; ensure every stated attribute is captured.
content: During extraction, if the source message explicitly enumerates several traits or reasons (for example 'brave, selfless, down-to-earth'), preserve each listed attribute in the memory content, either as a full list or as separate memory entries. Do not replace the list with a single broader trait such as 'leadership' that drops some of the stated qualities.
Before ADD, check whether the same subject already has a memory covering some of those traits; if so, UPDATE or MERGE to add the missing stated traits instead of creating a partial duplicate.
Stop after capturing all explicitly stated traits; do not add inferred qualities that are not present in the source text.

candidates.solves: When a user explicitly lists multiple distinct traits or reasons for liking, admiring, or evaluating someone, extraction often condenses them into one broader trait and drops the rest, leaving later questions about omitted qualities unanswered. This Skill applies whenever a source message enumerates two or more separate qualities as reasons (e.g., 'brave, selfless, down-to-earth') and a preference/admiration memory is being built or updated. It does not apply when only one trait is named or when the missing information would require inference beyond the stated text.

payload.name: Preserve explicit list items in extraction
payload.description: When a message explicitly names two or more distinct items (topics, activities, preferences, people, places) and an extraction candidate would summarize only a subset, require the candidate to include every named item.
content: During extraction, if a source message explicitly names multiple distinct items in a list, include each named item in the candidate content; do not replace the list with a paraphrase that omits any of them.
Preserve the full explicit list even when a shorter summary seems adequate; the listed facts are the evidence.
Stop once all explicitly named items are present; do not add unlisted details or expand the list.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes paraphrase a user's explicit list and drop one or more named items, so a later question asking about that detail finds no memory. This Skill applies when a single source message explicitly names two or more distinct items (e.g., 'dreams and life', 'hiking and swimming') and the candidate content would otherwise summarize a subset. It does not apply when the source contains no explicit enumeration, or when the candidate already includes every named item.

payload.name: Preserve Enumerated Items in Extracted Recommendations
payload.description: When a source message explicitly lists concrete items within a recommendation or offer and a memory candidate would collapse them into a generic phrase, use this Skill to keep each named item.
content: If a source message explicitly enumerates concrete items as part of a recommendation or offer (for example, 'acrylic paints, brushes, a canvas/paper, and a palette'), preserve each named item in the memory candidate as a compact list. Do not replace the enumeration with a generic placeholder such as 'supplies' that loses answerable facts.
Include only items explicitly stated in the message; do not infer additional items. If the candidate already contains the full enumeration, do not modify it. Stop once the named items are captured.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes reduce an explicit item list to a generic phrase (e.g., 'recommend supplies'), making later questions about which specific items were recommended unanswerable. This Skill applies when a future session contains a message where one speaker recommends or offers concrete enumerated items and a memory candidate is being built from it; the candidate must keep each named item. It does not apply when the message only mentions a category or topic without enumerating concrete items, or when the generic phrase already reflects the full content.

payload.name: Split Multi-Claim Messages During Extraction
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message contains both a factual event and an explicit subjective reaction, feeling, or evaluation about it; create separate durable candidates instead of one merged summary.
content: During extraction, when one message states multiple distinct durable claims—such as a narrated event plus the speaker's explicit subjective reaction or feeling about it—create one candidate per claim; do not merge them into a single event summary.
Include subjective statements only when the speaker explicitly states them in the message; preserve their meaning without adding interpretation.
Stop once every explicit distinct claim has its own candidate; do not infer unstated facts or expand beyond the message.

candidates.solves: General failure mechanism: extraction creates one summary candidate per message, dropping explicitly stated subjective/affective claims, so later questions about feelings cannot be answered. Applies to future sessions where a single message contains both a factual event and an explicit subjective reaction or evaluation; the skill splits them into separate candidates. Does not apply when a message contains only one claim or when the feeling is implied rather than explicitly stated.

payload.name: Extract-each-enumerated-goal-or-preference
payload.description: When a speaker message lists multiple distinct durable goals, preferences, or plans in one utterance, extract each item as a separate candidate or include all items in one candidate's content instead of dropping the unmentioned portion while enriching an existing memory.
content: During extraction, when one message explicitly enumerates two or more distinct durable facts (goals, preferences, plans, aspirations), create one candidate per distinct fact or make sure every distinct fact appears in the candidate content; do not let the enrichment of an existing memory omit the other items.
Stop after capturing the distinct durable items: ignore evaluative filler, examples, or transient remarks that do not add a new durable fact.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction can silently drop distinct durable facts when a single utterance lists several goals or preferences and only the part related to an existing memory is captured. This Skill applies to future sessions where a speaker enumerates multiple distinct durable goals/preferences in one message and one segment matches an earlier memory; the extractor should preserve each distinct item. It must not be applied to messages containing a single fact, or to rhetorical/evaluative filler that the base extraction already ignores.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated advice items during extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory from a message that gives the same person multiple distinct pieces of advice, criteria, or requirements, ensure every separate item is preserved in the candidate content.
content: During extraction, if one message contains several distinct recommendations for the same subject (e.g., 'make sure X', 'look for Y', 'it's important that Z'), include each distinct item in the candidate content.
If all items do not fit compactly in one preference/event memory, create separate candidates instead of omitting any item.
Treat phrases like 'make sure', 'it's important that', 'look for', 'avoid', 'must', and 'should' as introducing a separate requirement that must survive summarization.
Do not require verbatim copying or exhaustive inclusion of non-essential exposition; apply only to distinct requirements stated for the subject.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes condenses a message listing multiple distinct advice items and drops one, so later Q&A lacks that claim. This applies when a future message states several separate recommendations for the same subject and a memory is written from it: preserve each item. It does not apply to a single cohesive statement, unrelated details, or verbatim copying; do not expand scope unnecessarily.

payload.name: Preserve enumerated items in extraction
payload.description: When extracting or updating a memory from a statement that explicitly lists multiple distinct elements (e.g., 'growth, improvement, and confidence'), preserve each distinct element instead of paraphrasing the list into a single covering term.
content: If the source statement explicitly enumerates two or more distinct items (attributes, outcomes, examples, preferences), keep every distinct item in the candidate content or memory update; do not merge or paraphrase them into one broader term that drops any element.
When the list items are true synonyms or the paraphrase covers all enumerated meanings, compression is acceptable; only preserve when dropping any element would lose information.
During CRUD, when editing an existing memory that already captures a partial list, ADD/UPDATE it to include the missing enumerated items rather than writing a separate overlapping memory.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes paraphrase or compress a clause that explicitly lists several distinct elements, silently dropping one or more items (e.g., 'growth, improvement, and confidence' becoming 'growth and development'). This is repairable by requiring extraction to preserve each distinct enumerated item. Apply when a speaker explicitly enumerates multiple distinct attributes, outcomes, or examples in one statement and the candidate memory is being created or updated. Do not apply to ordinary paraphrase where items are synonyms and no distinct element is lost.

payload.name: Capture Habitual Item Asides in Extraction
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a user turn mixes a dominant activity with a brief aside naming a concrete item used habitually ('often', 'for fun'), create a separate compact candidate for the aside instead of dropping it.
content: During candidate extraction, scan each user turn for short asides that name a concrete object or item used in a recurring practice (e.g., an item the speaker puts on or uses with someone 'for fun', 'often', 'always').
When such an aside appears, emit it as its own compact candidate with an appropriate memory kind, even if the turn's main content is already being enriched into an existing memory.
Stop after capturing the aside: do not expand it into a full narrative, and skip it if it is a one-time occurrence or the item is already recorded in the memory being updated.

candidates.solves: Extraction can collapse a turn into its dominant activity and drop a small recurring item detail later questions may target. Use when a future turn pairs a main activity with a brief habitual aside naming a concrete object (e.g., an item 'often' put on someone); make the aside its own candidate. Not for one-off mentions, fully extracted multi-fact turns, or asides already in the targeted memory.

payload.name: Preserve Separate Memories for Struggle and Success
payload.description: Use when a construction candidate or memory decision involves a single message that explicitly reports both a difficulty/struggle and a positive outcome/achievement, to avoid losing the positive fact by merging.
content: During extraction, keep both the challenge and the positive outcome in the candidate content when a single message explicitly states both. During CRUD, do not merge them into one memory that records only the struggle; create separate memories (e.g., one event for the challenge, one event for the achievement) unless the positive statement is not a real result.

Split only when both facets are explicitly supported by the message. If the message states only one facet, or the positive wording is a future plan, preference, or neutral comment rather than a result, keep a single memory to avoid over-splitting.

candidates.solves: Fixes construction losing an explicitly stated positive outcome when the same message also reports a struggle, because both are collapsed into one memory that keeps only the struggle. Applies to future messages where one utterance explicitly reports both a difficulty and an achievement/positive result; create separate memories. Not applicable when the message only has one facet or the positive wording is a plan/preference/neutral comment rather than a real result.

payload.name: Preserve all enumerated items during extraction
payload.description: When a source message lists multiple distinct traits, reasons, or motivations (joined by 'and' or commas), keep every listed item in extraction candidates and any memory update; do not drop an item unless it restates the same fact.
content: During extraction, when a message states several distinct facts in a list or conjunction (e.g., 'passionate about A and B' or 'because of X, Y, and Z'), preserve every enumerated item in the candidate; do not omit an item as redundant unless the speaker's wording clearly restates a single fact.

During CRUD, when an ADD or UPDATE targets a memory that lacks one of the items enumerated in the source message, include the missing item in the new or merged content; never let a later version drop a detail that remains supported by evidence.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes summarize away one item from an enumerated list of traits, reasons, or motivations, so later memory cannot answer questions about the dropped item. This Skill applies whenever a future message lists multiple distinct attributes or motives that should all be recorded; it does not apply when the listed items are redundant paraphrases of a single fact or when the message contains no enumerable facts.

payload.name: Preserve all explicitly enumerated facts about an object
payload.description: When a user message explicitly lists multiple purposes, functions, uses, or attributes of a single object or plan and a memory candidate is being extracted or updated from that message.
content: If one message explicitly enumerates several purposes, uses, or attributes of the same object or plan, include every enumerated item in the candidate; do not keep only one item or summarize away the rest.
Name the object exactly as the evidence names it; do not replace it with a different object inferred from context.
When updating an existing memory with an explicit list, preserve the full list from the new evidence while still removing facts the new evidence contradicts.

candidates.solves: Memory construction can fail when a candidate summary drops some of several explicitly enumerated facts about an object or plan, or when it substitutes a different object than the one named in the evidence. This Skill applies to future sessions where one message lists multiple purposes, uses, functions, or attributes of the same item and that message is the source for extraction or update. It does not apply when the message makes a single general claim, when the message concerns separate unrelated objects, or when an existing memory is merely reworded without introducing a new enumerated list.

payload.name: Extract distinct facts per message during candidate generation
payload.description: When extracting candidates from a session and a later user message contains a new durable fact about a subject already mentioned in an earlier message, extract that fact as its own candidate instead of reusing or extending the earlier candidate.
content: During candidate extraction, treat each user message independently: identify every durable fact it states, even if the same subject or vehicle appears in an earlier message.

If a later message adds a distinct event or state (e.g., an item breaking down, a purchase, an accident) not present in the earlier extraction, create a separate candidate for it rather than reusing or merging it into the candidate from the earlier message.
Do not create duplicate candidates when the later message only restates or elaborates a fact already captured in an earlier candidate.

candidates.solves: During candidate extraction, distinct durable facts from different user messages in the same session can be collapsed into one candidate, so a later message's new fact (e.g., an item breaking down) never becomes a memory. This Skill applies when a later user message states a new event or state about a subject already mentioned earlier in the same session, and extraction may reuse an earlier candidate. It does not apply when the later message merely restates or elaborates a fact already captured in an earlier candidate.

payload.name: ExtractEachDistinctFactAsSeparateCandidate
payload.description: When a single message contains both an already-known fact and a new distinct fact (especially a purchase/event with a relative time), split them into separate extraction candidates; do not let the known fact absorb the new one.
content: During candidate extraction, emit one candidate per distinct factual claim in a message; do not bundle a new event/purchase under an already-known ownership or state fact.

Before SKIPping any candidate because its subject is already in memory, check the full message for another claim carrying new information (e.g., a purchase with a relative time); if found, create a separate candidate for that new fact and resolve its relative time to the concrete date from the message timestamp.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes bundles a new fact (e.g., a purchase with a relative date) into a candidate whose dominant claim is already known, causing a legitimate SKIP that silently drops the new fact. The Skill applies when a future message restates an already-memorized fact in the same sentence or turn as a distinct new event/purchase; it requires emitting one candidate per distinct claim so the new fact survives. It must not apply to messages that contain only a single claim or to candidates that genuinely add no new information, where SKIP remains correct.

payload.name: Preserve All Explicitly Enumerated Items in Extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message that explicitly enumerates multiple distinct reasons, strategies, preferences, or steps, preserve every listed item and do not add any unlisted detail.
content: When a source message explicitly lists multiple distinct items (reasons, strategies, preferences, steps), create one candidate per listed item, or one candidate containing the complete explicit list; never drop a listed item.
Before accepting the candidate, compare it against the source: every distinct item in the enumeration must be represented; if any is missing, revise the candidate.
Do not add any strategy, reason, preference, or activity that is not stated in the source message.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly lists multiple distinct reasons, strategies, preferences, or steps in one message, extraction tends to drop one listed item and may invent an unsupported one. This applies to future messages with explicit enumerations; preserve every listed item and add nothing unlisted. Not for single-fact messages or implied inferences.

payload.name: extract_ordinal_enumerated_traits
payload.description: When a user message lists multiple entities with ordinal labels (oldest, second, third, youngest, etc.) and assigns each a distinct personality or attribute, extract one memory candidate per entity during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message enumerates entities using ordinal descriptors (oldest, second, third, youngest, etc.) and gives each its own attribute, create one separate candidate per enumerated item.
Each candidate must preserve the entity type (e.g., pet, fur baby), the ordinal/positional descriptor, and the stated trait or attribute for that specific item.
Do not create per-item candidates for general group statements that do not assign distinct attributes to each enumerated member; stop after the explicitly enumerated items.

candidates.solves: The construction extractor omits candidates when a single user message enumerates several distinct items with ordinal labels (e.g., oldest, second, third, youngest) and assigns each a separate attribute, so all those facts are lost. The skill applies when such an ordinal enumeration appears in one message and each item has its own trait. It does not apply to group-level statements ('they are all playful') or to enumerations without per-item attributes.

payload.name: Extract-all-items-from-enumerated-statements
payload.description: Apply during candidate extraction when a single speaker message enumerates multiple distinct durable facts of the same category (e.g., activities, events, preferences, goals); capture each listed item so no stated fact is dropped.
content: During candidate extraction, if a message lists multiple distinct durable facts of the same category (e.g., 'studying, attending workshops, and networking'), create one candidate per listed item, or a single candidate that explicitly names every listed item; do not extract only the first or most salient item.
Limit extraction to the items actually asserted in the message; do not infer additional facts, complete partial lists, or expand the enumeration beyond what the speaker stated.

candidates.solves: Extraction frequently collapses an enumerated list in one message into a single candidate that captures only the most salient item, leaving other stated durable facts missing from memory. This Skill applies when a future message explicitly lists multiple distinct facts of the same category (activities, events, preferences, goals) that all merit memory; it requires capturing each item. It must not apply to messages where listed items are illustrative examples or where only one item is asserted as a durable fact, and it does not require exhaustive expansion beyond the speaker's own enumeration.

payload.name: Extract travel-location state memories
payload.description: During extraction, apply when a participant mentions a past vacation, trip, or travel photo with a named place and a time period, and no location-state or event candidate exists for that mention.
content: During candidate extraction, convert explicit travel/vacation mentions into state/event candidates: record that the speaker was at the named place during the stated time period, resolving relative time from the session timestamp.
If the named place is a city, include its unambiguous country in the same memory; do not guess when the city name maps to more than one country.
Stop after one candidate per distinct place-and-time mention; do not add candidates for places shown in photos or mentioned only as context without claiming the speaker was there.

candidates.solves: Travel or vacation statements that anchor a speaker to a specific place and time are often skipped during candidate extraction, leaving later questions about the speaker's location unanswerable. This Skill applies when a participant describes a past trip, vacation, or travel photo with a named place and a time reference. It must not apply when a place is mentioned without claiming the speaker was there, or when the named city's country is ambiguous.

payload.name: Aggregate-repeat-place-visits
payload.description: When a message mentions a visit to a place and an earlier distinct visit to the same place is already known, create a memory with the total visit count.
content: During candidate extraction, when the current message reveals a subject's visit to a specific place (city/country) and the session history or existing memory already contains a distinct earlier visit by the same subject to that same place at a different time, add an additional compact memory stating the total number of visits to that place (e.g., '<subject> has been to <place> N times'). Use memory kind 'state' or 'event' as appropriate. Do not add this aggregate when only one visit is known, when the two mentions refer to the same visit, or when the total count is already recorded; stop once the count is stated without enumerating each trip.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that repeated visits to the same place are stored only as separate event memories, leaving count questions like 'how many times has X been to Y?' unanswerable from memory. This applies when a later message reveals the same subject visiting the same city/country at a different time than an already-recorded visit. It must not apply when only one visit is known, when the two mentions refer to the same visit, or when the total count is already stored.

payload.name: Implied venue locations in trip plans
payload.description: When extracting or updating a plan/event memory about a trip to a named major venue with widely known location(s), include the implied states or city, unless the user already states the location.
content: During extraction or any update of a plan/event memory, if the destination is a major, well-known venue whose location is common knowledge and the user did not state it, add the venue's canonical location(s) (e.g., state or city) to the memory content.
Stop after adding the canonical known location(s); do not infer locations for obscure or ambiguous venues, and do not add any location the source message does not support.

candidates.solves: Plan/event candidates often record a named destination while dropping its implicit location, so later 'which states might they be in' questions cannot be answered from memory. This applies when a future session mentions a trip to a major venue with widely known locations, requiring those implied states to be stored during extraction. It does not apply when the user already specifies the location or when the venue's location is not common knowledge.

payload.name: Propagate established location to later activity events
payload.description: When extracting an event memory for an activity or discovery and the speaker's current location was set in an earlier message of the same conversation or recent session, include that location in the memory content.
content: Before finalizing an event candidate, scan prior turns for an explicit location associated with the speaker's ongoing trip or stay.
If the activity in the current message occurs during that same stay and no different location is mentioned, add the location to the candidate content (e.g., 'in <location>').
Do not add a location when the message states a different location, when the event is generic with no temporal/spatial tie to the established stay, or when no location anchor exists.

candidates.solves: Extraction often captures later activity or discovery messages without the location established in an earlier turn, producing memories that cannot answer 'where' questions. This skill applies when a speaker's current location (trip/stay) was set in a prior message and a subsequent message describes an activity or discovery from that same stay; it does not apply when the message specifies a different location or the activity has no clear link to the established location.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitQuotedClauses
payload.description: When constructing memory from a message containing a speaker's direct quoted statement, before accepting an extraction candidate, check that every explicit claim in the quoted text is represented, not only a paraphrase summary.
content: During extraction, when a source message is a direct quote (e.g., "John said ..."), compare the candidate memory content against the quoted utterance claim-by-claim.

If the candidate omits any explicit claim, especially a recommendation or assessment such as "you won't regret it," revise the candidate to include that claim, either in the same memory or as a separate memory entry.
Stop once all explicit claims are covered; do not add inferred implications or expand beyond the quoted text.

candidates.solves: The general failure is extraction candidates that paraphrase a speaker's quoted utterance and silently drop an explicit claim, causing later questions about that exact statement to be unsupported. This applies to future construction sessions where a message contains a direct quote with several distinct assertions, including evaluative or persuasive statements that a later question may target. It must not apply to ordinary conversational summaries that are not direct quotes or to exhaustively expanding paraphrase with inferred or general-knowledge content.

payload.name: Attribute relayed condition to the patient, not the speaker
payload.description: Use when extracting memories from a message where the speaker relays or acknowledges a fact about another participant's condition (e.g., a doctor's assessment said to the patient). Attribute the memory to that participant, not the speaker; keep separate subjects in separate candidates.
content: During extraction, when a message reports or acknowledges a condition fact about someone other than the speaker (e.g., 'the doctor said it's not too serious' in response to that person), create a separate state memory for that person, with the speaker only as source.
Resolve subject from pronouns and prior turns: 'your injury' refers to the addressee; a named person refers to that person. Do not merge facts about different subjects into one memory candidate.
If the same turn also contains the speaker's own state, emit distinct candidates per subject. Stop expanding further once each referenced person's fact has its own candidate.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often stores a fact about another participant's condition under the speaker, so the patient's state is missing. This skill applies when a message relays or acknowledges a doctor's or other assessment about the addressee or a named third party (e.g., John tells Tim 'the doctor said it's not too serious' after Tim's injury) and requires a separate memory attributed to that party. It does not apply when the message only describes the speaker's own condition or when the subject is already unambiguous.

payload.name: Extract first-person group behavior statements
payload.description: When a speaker uses first-person language to state a durable fact about their own or their group's behavior (e.g., 'we back each other up'), extract a candidate memory even if the statement appears inside a reply with thanks or filler.
content: During extraction, scan each message for explicit first-person statements about the speaker's own or their group's persistent behavior, traits, or approach (e.g., 'we back each other up', 'we won't quit').

When such a statement is found, create one durable candidate memory (typically a state or relationship) capturing the behavior, even if the statement is embedded in a reply that also contains thanks, pleasantries, or reactions to prior turns.
Do not create a candidate for transient, conversational, or purely reactive content (e.g., 'thanks', 'that's great') that does not state a durable fact.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that candidate extraction misses durable first-person statements about the speaker's or their group's behavior when they are embedded in conversational replies. This Skill applies when a future message contains an explicit first-person plural or singular statement of persistent behavior or approach (e.g., how a team handles tough opponents) that should become a memory. It does not apply to transient reactions, greetings, or purely conversational content that states no durable fact.

payload.name: Extract implied death from euphemistic loss language
payload.description: When a message describes someone with euphemistic permanent-loss phrases (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here'), use those cues during candidate extraction to record the implied state (likely deceased) as a hedged fact.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker refers to someone with euphemistic permanent-loss language—such as 'will never be able to support me' or 'I miss him/her here'—infer the implied state (likely deceased) and record it with hedged wording (e.g., 'likely no longer alive') instead of only the literal limitation.

Only apply this inference when the phrasing strongly implies permanent absence (e.g., 'never' combined with 'miss'); for temporary incapacity, mere distance, or estrangement, record only the literal limitation.
Do not state death as certain unless the message explicitly confirms it, and keep the memory evidence-bound by referencing the euphemistic phrase that supports the implication.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction candidates omit strongly implied facts when the source uses euphemistic loss language, so later memory-based answers cannot address questions about that implied state. This Skill applies when a user describes someone with permanent-loss euphemisms (e.g., 'will never be able to support me' plus 'I miss him here') and a future question may ask whether that person is alive. It must not apply when the language only indicates temporary incapacity, distance, or estrangement, which do not imply death.

payload.name: Preserve_short_speaker_quotes_during_extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates from a message that contains a short, distinctive verbatim quote from a speaker about an event or plan, preserve the exact quoted phrase in a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message contains a short (roughly 2-15 words) verbatim quote from a speaker that is a standalone statement about an event or plan, create a memory candidate that includes the exact quoted phrase (as event or state memory), in addition to any abstract event/relationship summary.

Limit to one quote memory per speaker-message pair, only when the quote is distinctive enough that a future question could ask 'what did X say about Y'; skip generic, long, or conversational filler utterances.

candidates.solves: General failure mechanism: extraction summarizes a speaker's words into abstract event/relationship memories and drops the verbatim quote, so later questions asking for exact wording cannot be answered. Applies to future construction sessions where a message contains a short, distinctive, attributable quote about an event or plan. Does not apply to messages without direct quotes, long/ordinary statements, or questions requiring only gist.

payload.name: Extract Anaphoric Entity Descriptions
payload.description: When a message contains a declarative reply identifying an object, person, or place via a pronoun/demonstrative (e.g., 'It's a ...', 'That's my ...'), and the referent is clear from prior context, extract a memory candidate.
content: During extraction, create a candidate when a speaker's short reply identifies or describes an entity with a pronoun/demonstrative, resolving the referent from the conversation history.
Record the fact as an event, state, or relationship memory, including the people involved (e.g., the speaker showed the described object to another participant) when the context supports it.
Do not extract if the statement is transient, purely subjective, or the referent is ambiguous; stop after capturing the core description.

candidates.solves: Extraction often misses durable facts stated in short anaphoric replies because it expects an explicit subject in the same sentence. Apply when a reply identifies/describes an entity via a pronoun (e.g., 'It's a ...', 'That's my ...') and the referent is clear; then extract one memory candidate for the entity and involved participants. Do not apply to transient/subjective remarks, ambiguous referents, or already-captured facts.

payload.name: Extraction Pronoun Referent Resolution
payload.description: When extracting a memory candidate and the source message uses a pronoun or demonstrative (this, it, they) to refer to an entity, resolve the referent from the current conversation before storing the candidate.
content: When a user message contains a pronoun/demonstrative ('this', 'it', 'they') that carries the main predicate of a candidate memory, resolve it to the entity the speaker is discussing in that turn; if a different entity appears nearby, do not attach the predicate to that entity.

Before accepting an extraction candidate, confirm the subject and object are explicit non-pronominal entities from the session; if the referent is uncertain, check only the current turn and immediately preceding messages, then choose the entity that best matches the predicate.

candidates.solves: Memory extraction sometimes resolves pronouns/demonstratives to the wrong nearby entity, storing a candidate about a different object than the one the speaker meant. This Skill applies when a user message uses 'this', 'it', or 'they' to refer to an entity and the candidate would record an attribute or motivation about it; it directs resolving the referent from the current turn and immediate context before storage. It does not apply when the message uses explicit nouns or the referent is unambiguous.

payload.name: Resolve-pronoun-referents-in-extraction
payload.description: When extracting a memory during construction and the user message uses 'this', 'it', or 'that' without a named entity, use to resolve the referent to the current topic and avoid substituting entities from earlier unrelated context.
content: When a candidate memory is extracted from a message containing a pronoun or demonstrative ('it', 'this', 'that'), resolve it to the entity explicitly under discussion in that same exchange or immediately preceding turns.

If the candidate's subject/object names an entity not present in the same message, verify it is the true antecedent of the pronoun; if it comes from an earlier, unrelated topic, replace it with the current referent.

Before committing a memory, check that the entity in the candidate content matches the literal referent in the evidence; discard or correct candidates whose object conflicts with the unambiguous antecedent.

candidates.solves: The failure is extraction assigning a pronoun or demonstrative to an entity from an earlier, unrelated part of the conversation, so the memory's subject/object does not match the evidence. It applies when a future user message uses 'this', 'it', or 'that' to refer to the object under discussion and the extracted candidate substitutes a stale entity. It does not apply when the entity is explicitly named in the message or the referent is unambiguous within the same sentence.

payload.name: Shared-habit confirmation to addressed person
payload.description: When a message uses 'same here, <Name>!' or 'me too, <Name>!' to confirm the addressed person shares the speaker's listed habits, extract memory candidates for both speaker and addressed person.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker says 'same here, <Name>!' or 'me too, <Name>!' and then lists practices/habits, create a separate state candidate with <Name> as subject containing the same listed practices, in addition to the speaker's candidate.
Only generate the addressee candidate when the sharing phrase clearly refers to the same listed practices; do not expand to other people or invent practices not explicitly named.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction omits memories for a named addressee when a speaker says 'same here, X!' or 'me too, X!' and lists practices, capturing only the speaker. Applies when a future message explicitly confirms the addressed person shares the listed durable practices: extract a candidate for both. Not applicable when agreement is about a one-off topic, or no addressee is explicitly named.

payload.name: Preserve co-participants in shared event memories
payload.description: When a message describes a travel, retreat, or activity shared with an explicit companion ('my partner and I'), keep the companion in the extracted event memory instead of attributing the event to the speaker alone.
content: During extraction, when a message states that the speaker and an explicitly identified companion (partner, friend, family member, named person) experienced a shared event such as travel, a retreat, or an activity, include all participants in the event candidate content (e.g., 'Jolene and her partner traveled...').
Do not reduce the event to the speaker alone just because the memory subject is the speaker; preserve explicit companion details that are part of the event.

When updating an existing event memory with new information confirming a companion shared it, amend the content to add the companion rather than creating a new memory. Stop after capturing the explicitly stated participants; do not infer companions from pronouns alone unless the message identifies them.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often drop explicit companions from shared events ('my partner and I traveled...' becomes 'Jolene attended...'), so later questions about joint travel cannot be answered. This applies when a future message describes an activity, trip, retreat, or experience shared by the speaker with a companion (e.g., 'my partner and I', 'my friend and I') and a memory candidate is being composed. It does not apply when the companion is only mentioned incidentally and did not share the event.

payload.name: Infer informal shared activities in relationship contexts
payload.description: When a user describes a past shared activity with a named partner or family member and explicitly mentions bonding, making memories, or closeness, extract an event/relationship memory even if the activity term is informal or generic; use strong contextual clues such as 'gaming' to infer the concrete activity.
content: During extraction, treat informal activity phrases (e.g., 'played games', 'gaming', 'used to do puzzles') as valid event/relationship candidates when the speaker links the activity to bonding, making memories, or spending time with a named person; do not skip them because the wording is generic.

Concretize the activity only when the wording strongly implies one specific type (e.g., 'gaming' → video games); if the activity is ambiguous (e.g., 'games' alone could be board or video), record the generic term as stated or skip instead of guessing.

Include the named person in the relationship and cite the bonding/memories purpose in the memory. Apply the same rule during CRUD: do not discard or over-merge such candidates merely because the activity was described informally.

candidates.solves: Extraction can fail to create any candidate when a shared activity is described informally (e.g., 'played games', 'gaming') even though the speaker ties it to bonding with a named person. This Skill applies when a future message describes a past shared pastime with a partner or family member and mentions closeness, memories, or bonding. It must not apply when the activity term is genuinely ambiguous with no clarifying clue, or when the activity is already named formally and the base extraction rule already covers it.

payload.name: Extract shared-activity relationship from casual enjoyment
payload.description: When a message says the speaker or a named person enjoys or regularly does an activity with another named person/pet, phrased casually like 'we have a great time doing X' or 'we love doing X together'.
content: During extraction, when a message states that the speaker or another named person enjoys or regularly does an activity together with a second named person or pet, expressed with casual mutual-enjoyment language (e.g., 'we have a great time doing X', 'we love X together'), create one relationship memory linking both participants with attributes for the activity and the enjoyment. Link the memory to the source message and use the session timestamp.

Do not create this memory for a single past occurrence (e.g., 'we went to the beach yesterday') unless the message also asserts a general preference; treat such one-off events as event memories. Create at most one memory per distinct (participants, activity) pair.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction skipped a durable shared-activity fact when it was phrased informally as mutual enjoyment ('we have a great time doing walks') rather than as a direct statement. This Skill applies to future messages in which a speaker states recurring, mutual enjoyment of an activity with another named entity, and instructs creation of a single relationship memory. It must not apply to one-off past activities or to a preference held by only one participant.

payload.name: PreserveSharedPartnerActivitiesInExtraction
payload.description: During extraction, when a speaker uses 'we' to describe an activity with a spouse/partner, generate a candidate memory that preserves the shared nature even if the partner is not named in the message.
content: During candidate extraction, treat first-person plural statements ('we', 'us', 'our') about activities as candidates for a shared-activity memory when the speaker has a known spouse/partner or the surrounding context identifies one.

Do not silently rewrite 'we' as the speaker alone: preserve the joint subject by using a relationship memory or an event memory whose content states the activity is shared with the spouse/partner, even if the partner's name is absent from the message.
Skip this rule for generic/impersonal 'we' and for statements where no specific companion is identifiable; leave first-person singular activity statements to the normal extraction path.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes drops or singularizes first-person plural statements, so memories of what a speaker and their spouse/partner do together are never created. Future questions asking about shared activities then have no supporting memory. This Skill applies when a speaker uses 'we' and the session context identifies the companion as a spouse/partner; it does not apply to generic or impersonal 'we' or to first-person singular statements about individual activities.

payload.name: Extract announced-event recipients from addressed messages
payload.description: When a user message directly addresses a named person (including the assistant) and announces a personal life event such as marriage, birth, or a move, extract a memory that records both the event and that it was told to that person.
content: During candidate extraction, when a user message addresses a named person (for example 'Hey Sam!') and announces a personal life event such as a marriage, birth, or move, extract the disclosure as a durable fact: the event occurred and that named person was told about it.
Record the audience explicitly in the event memory or as a separate relationship/event memory (e.g., 'Evan told Sam he got married'), citing the message as the source.
Stop at recipients explicitly addressed or named as the audience; do not infer other recipients from general context, and do not apply when no addressee is present.

candidates.solves: The general problem is that candidate extraction keeps the announced life event but drops the audience, so later questions such as 'who did X tell about Y?' become unanswerable. The Skill applies when a future user message names a specific addressee and announces a personal event like a marriage or a move. It must not apply when a message merely mentions an event without a named audience, because recording a recipient would fabricate evidence.

payload.name: Capture all participant roles in shared activities
payload.description: When extracting or updating a memory from a message where the speaker describes a shared activity or event (e.g., playdates, group outings) involving themselves and another party, and the source states what each party does.
content: During extraction, when a statement describes a joint activity with the speaker and another party (people or pets), capture the speaker's own explicit action or benefit as well as the other party's, rather than summarizing only the setting or the other party's behavior.
When updating or enriching an existing event memory with such a statement, preserve the speaker's role and add any newly stated action; do not let a topic-focused paraphrase replace it.
Stop after recording the explicitly stated actions of all named participants; do not infer additional roles or add unstated details.

candidates.solves: Extraction paraphrases sometimes collapse a jointly described activity and drop one participant's explicitly stated action—here the speaker's own role in a dog playdate was lost while the dogs' behavior was kept. This Skill applies when a future message describes a shared event or activity involving the speaker and another party (people or pets) and states what each does; it ensures both roles are captured in the extracted memory. It does not apply when the speaker only describes another party's activity or when the source does not state the speaker's own action.

payload.name: Extract companion activity statements
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement by the speaker about taking a walk, hike, or similar activity with a named companion (pet or person), extract a state or event candidate during extraction, even if the statement is in a closing or small-talk phrase.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states the speaker's activity with a named companion (e.g., walks, hikes, plays with), create one candidate memory even when the phrase is a sign-off or small talk.

Classify the candidate as event when the activity is one-off or explicitly planned, and as state when the phrasing implies a recurring habit; include the activity and companion in the memory content, and keep the source message ID.
Stop after the explicit activity: do not infer additional activities or habits beyond what the message states.

candidates.solves: Extraction often skips explicit activity statements with a named companion when they appear in casual sign-offs or small talk, leaving later questions about the speaker's activities unsupported. This Skill applies when a message explicitly claims the speaker's activity (walking, hiking, etc.) with a named companion. It does not apply when the companion is mentioned without an activity verb or the message is purely phatic.

payload.name: Extract explicit durations from group statements
payload.description: When a message states the speaker's past group involvement with an explicit duration, even if it also contains a question or filler, during extraction create a relationship/event candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message states the speaker's past involvement in a group or relationship with an explicit duration (e.g., 'we were teammates for four years'), create a relationship or event candidate capturing the speaker, the group, and the duration, even when the utterance also ends with a question or casual filler.

Treat the explicit duration alone as sufficient evidence for a candidate; do not require additional corroborating sentences. Do not apply this to statements about another person's experience or to turns without a factual predicate.

candidates.solves: This addresses the general failure mechanism where explicit duration facts about the speaker's past group involvement are skipped during extraction when the same utterance also contains a question or casual filler. It applies to future sessions when a message states something like 'We were teammates for four years' in first-person plural with an explicit time period. It must not apply to statements about another person's experience or to turns that contain no factual predicate.

payload.name: Multi-party first-person attribution
payload.description: When a multi-party conversation contains a message where a participant uses first-person language ('I', 'my', 'me') to state their own preference, opinion, or state, use the message's speaker as the memory subject during extraction and CRUD.
content: During extraction, read the speaker of each message and, for any first-person statement ('I', 'my', 'me', 'we'), set the memory subject to that speaker, never to another participant.
When a candidate combines statements from multiple speakers, split it into one candidate per speaker; do not merge different speakers' views into a single profile memory.
Before accepting an ADD/UPDATE, compare the candidate subject with the source speaker: if a first-person statement is attributed to someone else, correct the subject or reject the candidate.

candidates.solves: Generalizes extraction failures where a participant's self-expressed preference or opinion is stored under another participant's name, causing missing memories. Applies to future multi-party sessions in which a message uses first-person language ('I', 'my', 'me') to describe the speaker's admiration, preference, or state; the memory subject must be that speaker. Does not apply when the message explicitly attributes the statement to a different person (e.g., 'Tim loves LeBron'), where the named person is the subject.

payload.name: PreserveJointParticipantsWhenWeIsUsed
payload.description: When a user message describes an activity with first-person plural pronouns ('we', 'our') and the session establishes a specific partner/companion, include that companion in the event memory instead of attributing the activity to the speaker alone.
content: During extraction and update, when a user uses 'we'/'our' for an activity and a specific partner, spouse, or companion is established in the session, record the event with the speaker and that companion as co-participants.

Add the co-participant only if their identity is explicit or directly implied by recent context (e.g., wedding, honeymoon, 'my partner'); stop if 'we' is generic or no specific companion is identifiable.
Do not invent participants for unnamed or collective groups; keep the memory at the level of evidence.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of joint participants when event memories are built from first-person plural statements; applies to future sessions where a user says 'we' about an activity and a partner/spouse is known; does not apply when 'we' is generic or no specific co-participant can be identified.

payload.name: Extract entity status from explicit condition statements
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a user or assistant explicitly states the current condition, performance, or status of a specific entity they own or manage (e.g., 'the store's doing great', 'the project is on track'), use this Skill to create a state memory.
content: When a message from any participant explicitly states the current condition or performance of a specific entity they own or manage, extract a `state` memory candidate with the entity, the stated condition, the speaker, and the message timestamp.
Apply this even if the statement appears in casual greetings or small talk; do not wait for a later question about the entity.
Do not extract vague sentiment without a specific entity, and do not infer conditions that are not explicitly stated.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction omits explicit statements about an entity's current condition (e.g., 'The store's doing great!'), leaving later questions like 'How is Gina's store doing?' unsupported. This Skill applies when a participant states the status of an entity they own or manage, and records it as a state memory. It does not apply to vague opinions without a specific entity, already-captured facts, or hypothetical/future conditions.

payload.name: Extract explicit future activity proposals
payload.description: During extraction, when a speaker states a concrete proposed future activity with another person, including tentative or alternative phrasings (e.g., 'maybe we can ... or ...'), create a plan candidate.
content: In the extraction stage, when a message contains a concrete proposal for a future activity involving the speaker and another person (e.g., 'we can do X together', 'maybe we can Y or Z'), create a single `plan` candidate capturing the proposed action(s) and participants, even if phrased tentatively.
If the proposal offers multiple alternatives as one intention (e.g., 'X or Y'), keep them in one plan candidate rather than dropping the message.
Skip only vague or purely hypothetical remarks (e.g., 'someday we might...') and re-statements of already-stored plans.

candidates.solves: General failure mechanism: extraction misses an explicit future activity proposal because it is phrased tentatively or with alternatives, leaving the memory without a plan. This applies when a future construction session processes a message where a speaker concretely proposes doing something together (with options). It must not apply to vague hypothetical statements or to clearly past or completed events, which are not plans.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Resource Suggestions
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit suggestion or recommendation from one speaker to another to check out a specific resource (e.g., a book, article, website) for insights on a topic, extract it as a candidate event memory during construction.
content: During extraction, if any message explicitly recommends or suggests that the main user (or another named speaker) consult a specific, named resource (book, article, website, video, etc.) for insights on a topic, create a candidate event memory capturing: who made the suggestion, to whom, the resource mentioned, and the topic it addresses.

Do not skip such candidates merely because the recommended resource appears only as advice, because the message is from a speaker other than the main user, or because the topic (e.g., a dream) is personal.

Stop after one candidate per suggestion; do not expand to every noun or mentioned item. If no concrete resource is named, or the message only asks for a recommendation without making one, no candidate is needed.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that explicit suggestions of concrete resources are missed during extraction, so later questions about who recommended what cannot be answered. This Skill applies when a speaker explicitly tells another to check out a named resource for insights on a topic. It does not apply when no concrete resource is named or when the message merely asks for a recommendation.

payload.name: Enumerated Routine Steps Extraction
payload.description: When a speaker answers a question by enumerating steps of a routine or care process, extract each step as a separate memory candidate and capture any overall evaluation.
content: During extraction, if a speaker (not the user) answers a question by listing multiple components of a routine or care process (often using imperatives like 'keep...', 'feed...', 'make sure...'), create a separate candidate memory for each component, attributed to the speaker as a preference, state, or plan.
Also extract any explicit overall evaluation of the process (e.g., 'not tough', 'easy') as its own candidate memory.

Stop after the enumerated items and the evaluation; do not add inferred steps. Do not apply when the speaker is giving a direct command to the user without describing their own practice, or when the items are one-time events.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that extraction misses all candidate memories when a speaker describes a routine or care process through an imperative enumeration, leaving no durable record. Applies to future sessions where a speaker answers a question with two or more direct steps (e.g., 'keep clean', 'feed properly', 'give light') and possibly an overall judgment. Does not apply to direct commands in an ongoing interaction or to transient event descriptions.

payload.name: Extract Activity Domain Disclosures
payload.description: When a user explicitly states what they write about, study, research, or recommend, extract a preference or state memory for that activity domain during candidate extraction.
content: During extraction, treat explicit first-person statements of ongoing activities (writing about, studying, researching, recommending, focusing on) as candidate memories, even if phrased conversationally in a list.
Emit one memory using preference or state that records the activity and its subjects; do not require a follow-up question before extracting.
If an existing candidate or memory already covers the same fact, skip; otherwise always generate the candidate so the fact is preserved.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage occasionally emits zero candidates from a message where the user explicitly states an ongoing activity domain (e.g., what they write about, study, or recommend), causing later questions about that domain to be unanswerable. This skill applies when a future message contains an explicit first-person statement of such an activity; it should then generate a preference/state memory capturing the activity and subjects. It must not apply to messages that only mention a subject with no stated activity or personal involvement.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice from one speaker to another
payload.description: When a message contains explicit advice, recommendation, or instruction from one speaker to another about how to do something, and that advice is not already captured in memory, extract it as a candidate memory.
content: During extraction, treat explicit advice or directives from one speaker to another as a candidate memory (e.g., relationship or event) that records who advised whom and the actionable content.
Only extract when the advice is specific and actionable, not for generic pleasantries, questions, or non-directive opinions.
Bind the candidate to the source message and the recipient so later questions about 'what advice did X give Y' can retrieve it.

candidates.solves: This solves extraction omissions where explicit advice from one speaker to another is not turned into a candidate memory, causing later questions about that advice to be unanswerable. It applies when a message directly advises or instructs a named recipient on how to do something (e.g., 'Make sure you watch other people's videos first...'). It does not apply to general statements, opinions, or rhetorical suggestions that are not actionable directives, nor to advice that is already represented in existing memories.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Advice Between Speakers
payload.description: When a user message records one character giving explicit advice or a recommendation to another, extract it as a relationship/event memory during extraction.
content: During extraction, for each user message that contains one character giving explicit advice, recommendation, or guidance to another character, create a candidate memory preserving the advice near-verbatim.

Record the advisor as the source and the advisee as the target; use memory type 'relationship' for the advisor-advisee link or 'event' for the act of advising, and link the candidate to the source message ID.
Only apply when the advice is explicitly stated; do not infer advice from tone, implied intent, or general encouragement without a concrete directive.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage skips direct advice one character gives to another in a user turn, so later questions asking for that advice find no supporting memory. Apply to future sessions where a user message contains an explicit advice or recommendation directed from one speaker to another and a question may target it. Do not apply to third-person narration, implied sentiment, or comments with no concrete directive.

payload.name: Extract explicit action commitments as plan memories
payload.description: When a message contains a speaker's explicit commitment or offer to perform a specific future action for someone, apply this Skill during extraction to ensure a plan memory is created.
content: During extraction, when a speaker states an explicit commitment or offer to perform a concrete future action for another person (e.g., 'I will write it down and mail it to you'), create a plan memory capturing the action, recipient, and any time reference in the message.
Do not create a plan memory for hypothetical, conditional, or non-committal statements (e.g., 'I could help', 'I sometimes share recipes') unless they contain a definite future action.

candidates.solves: The general failure is that explicit future commitments made by a speaker during conversation are not extracted as plan memories, leaving later questions about the speaker's intended actions unanswered. This Skill applies when a future session contains a concrete offer or promise to perform an action for someone (e.g., 'I will write it down and mail it to you'); in that case extract a plan memory. It must not apply to hypothetical, conditional, or generic ability statements that do not commit the speaker to a specific future action.

payload.name: Extract explicit offers of help or support
payload.description: When a participant explicitly offers help, support, tips, or assistance on a specific topic to another participant, create a memory candidate for the offer.
content: During extraction, treat explicit offers of help, support, tips, or assistance directed at the other participant as memory-worthy facts.

Signal words include 'if you need', 'let me know', 'happy to help', 'just ask', or 'offer'; when such an offer names a concrete topic, create one relationship or event candidate capturing the offerer, the topic, and the recipient, linked to the source message.
Do not extract generic polite closings without a concrete offer (e.g., 'let me know if you need anything') or messages that merely thank or acknowledge the other participant.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction misses explicit offers of help, support, or tips, so later questions about the offer (e.g., 'What did Sam offer Evan?') cannot be answered from memory. Applies to future sessions where one participant makes a concrete offer of assistance or tips on a named topic; does not apply to generic pleasantries or mere thanks where no specific offer is extended.

payload.name: Extract explicit requests for help or discussion
payload.description: During extraction, when a message contains an explicit ask from one person to another for help, advice, or to discuss a specific topic, create an event candidate recording the ask as a distinct memory.
content: If a message contains an explicit request such as 'Can we talk about X?', 'Can you help me with X?', or 'Please help me with X', extract an event memory with subject as the speaker, content stating 'asked [recipient] for help with X' or 'asked [recipient] about X', and world_start set to the message timestamp.
Keep this request memory separate from any memory about the speaker's struggle or intention to reach out later; do not merge them.
Do not create a request memory when the message only expresses a need, difficulty, or future intention (e.g., 'I'm struggling' or 'I will reach out') without an explicit ask directed at a recipient.

candidates.solves: Extraction often captures a speaker's struggle or future intention but omits the explicit request itself, leaving the ask unrecorded and unanswerable later. This skill applies to any future message where a speaker explicitly asks another person for help, advice, or to discuss a specific topic (e.g., 'Can we talk about X?'). It must not apply when only a need, struggle, or intention to reach out is expressed without a direct request.

payload.name: Record advice details when offer contains tips
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a message contains an offer or plan plus concrete advice, tips, or steps; store the advice as its own memory instead of only logging the offer.
content: During extraction, if a speaker offers help or proposes a plan and also lists specific advice, tips, or steps, create a separate memory candidate for that advice (e.g., as an event or state) in addition to any memory for the offer or plan.
Do not let the offer memory absorb the advice: preserve the concrete details, such as the method or strategy recommended, because they are the durable facts.
Skip this when the advice is only a generic courtesy (e.g., 'let me know if you need help') with no substantive content.

candidates.solves: Extraction often records that someone offered help or a plan but drops the concrete advice stated in the same message, so later questions about the discussed strategies lack evidence. This Skill applies when a message combines an offer/plan with explicit tips or steps and the memory must keep the advice as its own fact. It does not apply to purely generic offers with no substantive advice, or when the advice is already captured in another candidate.

payload.name: Extract hedged suggestions as event memories
payload.description: When a participant gives advice or a suggestion to another participant, especially phrased as a question or with hedges like maybe/could/perhaps, use this during extraction to create an event candidate.
content: During extraction, when a speaker gives advice, a recommendation, or a suggestion to another speaker, create an event candidate even if the utterance is phrased as a question or uses hedges like 'maybe', 'could', 'perhaps', or 'might'.
Capture the speaker, the recipient, and the recommended course of action; if the advice refers to a condition or problem the recipient previously mentioned, include that context in the memory.
Stop after recording the suggestion; do not infer outcomes, acceptance, or additional facts beyond what the utterance states.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction misses suggestions phrased as hedged questions or tentative advice, leaving factual conversational events unrecorded. This Skill applies whenever one participant recommends an action to another, especially about the recipient's earlier-mentioned problem, in any future session. It does not apply to declarative general advice without a specific recipient or non-advice questions.

payload.name: Extract explicit advice as a memory candidate
payload.description: When extracting candidates from a conversation, if a message contains explicit advice or a suggestion from one named participant to another about a specific action, create a candidate for that advice.
content: Generate one extraction candidate for any clear, specific suggestion or directive from one named participant to another (e.g., 'keep doing X', 'you should try Y'); record it as an 'event' for the advice or as 'preference'/'state' if it reflects a stable inclination of the advisee.
Skip generic fillers, rhetorical statements, and advice lacking a named recipient or a specific action; do not create more than one candidate per advice speech act.
Do not infer acceptance or commitment unless the advisee later agrees; then add a separate 'plan' candidate for the advisee.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes skips explicit advice or suggestions from one participant to another, leaving later questions about what someone advised unanswerable. This Skill applies when a future message contains a clear directive or suggestion (e.g., 'keep doing X') from a named speaker to a named recipient.
